parts.title: An Introduction to Shri Atmasiddhi Shastra

items.q: What is the meaning and significance of the words Shri, Atma, Siddhi and Shastra?
a: Shri — The word Shri is used in front of something holy or sacred. It shows greatness, purity and divinity. By adding Shri before Atmasiddhi Shastra, it reminds us that this is not an ordinary book. It's a sacred scripture with divine wisdom written by an Enlightened Master, Shrimad Rajchandraji. It also shows our deep respect for the text and its author.

Atma means the soul — our true inner self that is eternal, full of knowledge and separate from the body and mind. The soul is pure and unchanging, but due to ignorance, we forget our real nature and think we are just the body or mind. The atma is the main subject of this scripture. The entire Shastra helps us to understand and realise who we truly are — the pure soul.

Siddhi means attainment, accomplishment, or realisation. In this context, it means achieving Self-realisation — realising and experiencing the soul directly. When a person gains Atma-Siddhi, it means he has attained knowledge of his true self and becomes free from ignorance and bondage. This is the ultimate goal of spiritual life.

Shastra means scripture or sacred text. It is a work that teaches truth and guides seekers on the spiritual path. A Shastra contains logical reasoning, examples, and explanations that help us understand deep spiritual ideas clearly. Shri Atmasiddhi Shastra is therefore a spiritual guide written in poetic form to lead seekers towards Self-realisation.

items.q: Mention any 3 benefits of the question-answer style of Shri Atmasiddhi Shastra for the reader. Mention any 3 spiritual texts that employ a similar style.
a: Three benefits:
1. Easy to understand — The question-answer format makes difficult spiritual ideas simple and clear. It helps readers understand each concept step by step.
2. Clears doubts — The disciple's questions are similar to the doubts that arise in our own minds. When the Guru answers them, our own doubts are also removed.

3. Creates interest and connection — The dialogue between the Guru and disciple keeps the reader interested and makes the scripture feel like a personal conversation. It helps us reflect deeply on each truth.
Three spiritual texts:
1. Bhagavad Gita — a dialogue between Lord Krishna and Arjun.
2. Upanishads — conversations between spiritual teachers and their disciples.
3. Samaysar — explains truths of the soul through questions and answers between the soul and right knowledge.

items.q: a) Who has written the mangalacharan of Shri Atmasiddhi Shastra? b) In the mangalacharan, what analogy is given for Shri Atmasiddhi Shastra and for P. Saubhagbhai? c) What is the meaning of Patit Jan Pavani and Adham Uddharini?
a: (a) The mangalacharan of Shri Atmasiddhi Shastra was written by Pujya Lalluji Muni.

(b) Shri Atmasiddhi Shastra is compared to a Kalpavruksha — a wish-fulfilling tree that grants the ultimate spiritual wish of Self-realisation to seekers. Pujya Saubhagbhai is compared to a garden or fertile land where this Kalpavruksha first grew, because the scripture was composed in response to his request.

(c) Patit Jan Pavani means the purifier or uplifter of fallen souls — one who frees people lost in ignorance and wrong beliefs. Adham Uddharini means the saviour of the lowly or the humble — one who uplifts even the most ignorant and unworthy beings towards the path of liberation.

items.q: Give any two reasons explaining the universal appeal of Shri Atmasiddhi Shastra.
a: 1. Applies to all, beyond religion or caste — Shri Atmasiddhi Shastra speaks about the soul, which is common to all living beings. Its message is not limited to any religion, sect, or community. It is for anyone seeking truth and peace.

2. Practical and experiential teaching — The Shastra does not just give theories. It shows a practical path for daily living and inner growth. It guides one to experience Self-realisation through right thinking, faith, and conduct, which makes it meaningful for people of all backgrounds and times.

parts.title: I. Answer in a few words.

items.q: Which is the most tangible way to understand the complex philosophy of the scriptures?
a: Through the guidance and teachings of a living Sadguru, who can explain, inspect, and clarify their true meaning.

items.q: What is the remedy shown in the first verse to end our suffering?
a: To realise the true nature of the Self through the teachings of the Enlightened Sadguru, who removes ignorance.

items.q: Who does Shrimad Rajchandraji, in verse 20, say has revealed the path of humility?
a: The completely detached Lords (Shri Vitrags) have revealed the path of humility (Vinay marg).

items.q: Through which word has Shrimad Rajchandraji remembered and glorified the humility of Shri Saubhagyabhai? What is the meaning of this word?
a: Through the word “Subhagya”, meaning fortunate or blessed one.

items.q: Mokshmarg (the path of liberation) is the integration of which two things?
a: The integration of right knowledge (Jnan) and right conduct (Kriya)-understanding and action guided by Self-realisation

parts.title: II. Identify and rectify the error in understanding in the statements below.

items.q: Shrimad Rajchandraji wants the mechanical ritualists and dry intellectualists to stop their religious activities.
a: He does not want them to stop religious activities, but to perform them with the right understanding and purpose, aligning rituals and knowledge with Self-realisation instead of ego or show.

items.q: A Sadguru has the highest knowledge of all the scriptures because He has read them.
a: Sadguru's mastery of scriptures arises from direct Self-realisation, not from mere reading. His understanding is experiential, revealing the essence of truth.

items.q: A Sadguru behaves the same with everyone due to His equanimity.
a: A Sadguru’s inner state remains equanimous, but His outer behaviour varies according to each disciple’s capacity and need. He may praise, correct, or remain silent — all with equal compassion.

items.q: When constant contact with Sadguru is not there, the seeker should contemplate upon spiritual scriptures of his own choice.
a: The seeker should study and contemplate only those scriptures prescribed by the Sadguru, and regularly give up personal opinions and prejudices while doing so.

items.q: The scriptures themselves mention that even a monk who has extensive knowledge of the scriptures may not attain liberation. Hence knowledge is not necessary, only rituals are enough.
a: Knowledge is essential, but it must be joined with inner detachment and right practice. Mere scholarship or ritualism without Self-awareness leads to delusion. Both knowledge and conduct are necessary for liberation.

parts.title: III. Answer in one or two sentences.

items.q: What are the two meanings of the word 'anant' (infinite) explained by Pujya Gurudevshri?
a: 1. Beginningless suffering- the soul has suffered since infinite time due to ignorance of the Self, and
2. Immeasurable intensity of sorrow- the suffering continues endlessly until Self-realisation ends it.

items.q: Write any two meanings of "Shri Sadguru Bhagwant" explained by Pujya Gurudevshri.
a: ‘Shri’ represents scripture, ‘Sadguru’ the living Guru, and ‘Bhagwant’ the Omniscient Lord- the Dev–Guru–Sastra triad.
My Sadguru is my Bhagwan- expressing total reverence and oneness between the Guru and the Divine.

items.q: What is the reason for Sadguru's state of desirelessness?
a: The Sadguru’s joy arises from the Self; having realised the inner source of bliss, He has no craving for external objects or circumstances, hence remains naturally desireless and content.

items.q: What is the most important difference between scripture and living Sadguru?
a: Scripture can instruct but not inspect, while a living Sadguru can personally guide, correct, and remove delusion in real time, tailoring the teaching to the disciple’s needs.

items.q: Even though living Sadguru has not attained absolute liberation, why is He needed to understand the true nature of the Jina?
a: Because only a living Sadguru can explain and make the state of the Jina (Jina-swarup) understandable and attainable to the seeker. Without His guidance, one may worship the Jinas outwardly but fail to grasp Their inner state of dispassion and omniscience.

items.q: What limitation of contact of Dev (Omniscient Lord) and Guru (Enlightened Mentor) is not there in Shastra (scriptures)?
a: The scriptures are always accessible- they can be read or heard anywhere, anytime, unlike the Dev, who is no longer present in this era, and the Guru, whose physical presence is limited by place and time. Hence, scripture serves as a support (adhar) until one meets the living Sadguru.

items.q: Why is the state described in verse 17 (Swachhand, mat, agrah taji, varte Sadgurulaksh) called samkit (right faith), even though there is no direct experience of the pure self here?
a: Because when one lives with faith, love, and surrender to the Sadguru’s command, that inner state becomes the immediate cause of direct Self-experience. Bhagwan calls it Samkit (Right Faith) since the seed of Self-realisation is already sown and its fruit is certain.

items.q: Why is an asadguru doubly harmful?
a: An asadguru is harmful both to himself and to his disciples: He binds intense deluding karma by pretending to be realised and exploiting disciples’ reverence. He misleads seekers, diverting them from the true path of liberation. Thus, he sinks in the ocean of saṁsāra and drags others with him.

items.q: What is Shrimad Rajchandraji's purpose behind describing the characteristics of a bigot (matarthi) in the next section (verses 24-33)?
a: Shrimad Rajchandraji’s purpose is not to criticise or condemn anyone, but to help sincere seekers recognise and remove sectarian or ego-driven tendencies within themselves. By describing the traits of a matārthī impartially (nirpakṣa), he provides a mirror for self-reflection, so that aspirants can avoid rigidity and return to the path of true seeking.

items.q: Why are the scriptures considered reliable?
a: Scriptures are considered reliable because they are the authentic words of realised beings who have directly experienced truth. They establish the existence and nature of the soul and non-soul and serve as a dependable guide for deserving seekers, especially when a living Sadguru is not available.

parts.title: IV. Answer in brief.

items.q: Explain how the path of humility leads one to liberation.
a: The path of humility, or vinay marg, is the foundation of spiritual progress in Sri Atmasiddhi Shastra. Shrimad Rajchandraji explains in verses 19 and 20 that true humility is not just outer politeness but an inner state of surrender, respect, and openness toward the Sadguru. When a disciple becomes humble, his ego softens and he becomes receptive to the Guru’s grace. Through this humility, he learns to obey the Guru’s ajna sincerely, which leads to right faith, self-realisation, and ultimately liberation.

The completely detached Lords, the Vitrag Bhagwans, have revealed humility as the root cause of liberation, understood only by a few fortunate souls. As said in verse 20, “Evo marg vinay tano bhakhyo Shri Vitrag, mul hetu e margno samje koi subhagya.” Humility melts pride and self-will, allowing the disciple to absorb the Guru’s wisdom and walk steadily on the path of liberation.

items.q: Why did Shrimad Rajchandraji specifically highlight maan (ego) as the primary foe, instead of krodh (anger) etc.", to encompass the obstacles to spiritual growth in verse 18?
a: Shrimad Rajchandraji specifically highlighted maan, or ego, as the primary foe in verse 18 because it is the root cause of all other inner enemies such as anger, deceit, and greed. Anger, pride, deceit, and greed are all forms of ego expressing itself in different ways. Among these, pride is the most subtle, powerful, and hardest to uproot. A person with ego does not easily accept guidance, correction, or surrender to a higher truth, which makes spiritual progress impossible.

Shrimad Rajchandraji wanted seekers to understand that ego prevents one from seeking refuge in the Sadguru, while humility opens the door to liberation. By destroying pride, all other passions naturally weaken. As he explains in verse 18, “Maanadi shatru maha, nij chhande na maray; jata Sadguru sharanma, alp prayase jaay,” meaning that the mighty inner enemies beginning with pride cannot be destroyed by one’s own effort, but when one takes refuge in the Sadguru, they disappear effortlessly. Hence, maan was emphasized to show that overcoming pride through surrender and humility is the key to conquering all spiritual obstacles.

items.q: Explain the quality of an atmarthi (true seeker) described in this section through verse 8 (Jya jya je je yogya chhe ...).
a: In verse 8 of Sri Atmasiddhi Shastra, Shrimad Rajchandraji beautifully describes the quality of a true seeker, or atmarthi, as one who acts with prudence, awareness, and balance. He says, “Jya jya je je yogya chhe, taha samajvu teh; tya tya te te achare, atmarthi jan eh,” meaning, “Wherever and whatever is appropriate, he understands it and acts accordingly – such a person is a true seeker.”

An atmarthi is not rigid or mechanical. He uses discriminative knowledge (vivek) to understand what is suitable at a given time, place, and circumstance, and then acts upon it sincerely. He is guided by wisdom, not by habit or emotion. Unlike the mechanical ritualist, who follows routine blindly, or the dry intellectualist, who stops at words and theories, the true seeker combines understanding with practice. He knows his strengths and limitations, remains aware of the world’s distractions, and adjusts his actions to stay aligned with the goal of self-realisation.

Thus, Shrimad Rajchandraji shows that an atmarthi is neither extreme nor careless—he is thoughtful, balanced, and ever alert, ensuring that every action supports his inner growth and leads him closer to liberation.

items.q: Why is it necessary to stop swachhand (self willed behaviour) in order to attain liberation, and why is it difficult to stop it? How does association with a living Sadguru help us get rid of it easily?
a: Stopping swachhand, or self-willed behaviour, is absolutely necessary for attaining liberation because self-will is the root of bondage. When a person follows his own opinions, moods, and preferences instead of truth or the Guru’s guidance, his actions are driven by ego. This ego strengthens attachment, pride, deceit, and greed, which in turn create new karmas and keep the soul bound to suffering. As Shrimad Rajchandraji says in verse 15, “Roke jiva swachhand to, pamey avashya moksh,” meaning that only when self-will is restrained can the soul surely attain liberation.

However, stopping swachhand is extremely difficult because it is an ancient and deeply ingrained habit. It feels natural to act according to one’s own views and emotions, and ego cleverly disguises itself as sincerity or righteousness. Therefore, even spiritual efforts often become guided by self-will rather than true surrender.

The association of a living Sadguru (pratyaksh Guru) makes this process easy and effective. In verse 16, Shrimad Rajchandraji explains, “Pratyaksh Sadguru yogthi, swachhand te rokay; anya upay karya thaki, praye bamano thay,” meaning that only through the living Sadguru’s company and guidance can self-will be restrained, while through other means it usually doubles. The Sadguru helps the disciple by pointing out hidden ego, giving clear and tailored instructions (ajna), and melting pride through love and compassion. His living presence inspires obedience and self-reflection, allowing the seeker to surrender his will joyfully. In this way, what is impossible through one’s own effort becomes effortless through surrender and association with the living Sadguru, leading the soul toward freedom and liberation.

items.q: Mention any two ways in which practising detachment etc. helps in attaining self-realisation. Mention any two benefits of detachment etc. if they are along with self-realisation.
a: Practising detachment and other noble virtues helps in self realisation in many ways. First, it purifies the mind by reducing passions like desire, pride, anger, and greed, allowing calmness and focus to develop. Second, it creates worthiness by weakening attachments and directing attention inward, helping the seeker cultivate love for the truth and readiness for self realisation. When detachment and such virtues accompany self realisation, they bring two major benefits. They stabilise the realised state, keeping awareness of the Self steady and free from distraction, and they speed up progress toward liberation by stopping new karmic bondage and helping old karmas to dissolve quickly. Shrimad Rajchandraji explains in verse 6 that detachment and similar virtues are meaningful when joined with self realisation and also serve as the means to attain it.

parts.title: V. Self-reflection and inner inquiry

items.q: Consider a recent instance of joy or sorrow. What did you believe its cause was? How does this belief align or contradict with the teaching from Atmasiddhi Shastra?
a: Recently I felt a deep sense of disappointment and sadness when my internship ended abruptly because of a miscommunication with my manager. I believed the cause of my sorrow was the situation itself, losing the chance to extend my role, continue learning, and strengthen my professional path. It felt unfair and outside my control. However, when I reflect through the teaching of Sri Atmasiddhi Shastra, especially from verse 1, I can see that this belief comes from identifying my happiness and worth with external events. Shrimad Rajchandraji explains that suffering arises not from outer situations but from ignorance of the true Self.

In truth, my pain did not come from the internship ending but from my attachment to it, to my plans, recognition, and expectations. The event only showed how dependent my peace was on outer conditions. The teaching reminds me that real joy and stability do not lie in circumstances but in staying centered in Self awareness. The internship’s end was temporary, but the peace within is constant. If I remain aware of the Self and detached from outcomes, no external loss or miscommunication can truly disturb me.

items.q: Which beliefs has the study of this section helped you correct, or reinforce? How is it going to benefit you?
a: Through the study of this section of Sri Atmasiddhi Shastra, I have begun to correct a few deep rooted beliefs that fuel my daily anxiety and self doubt. I used to believe that my peace depended on how well things went in my studies, work, and relationships, and that I could feel secure only when I was in control of situations. This constant need to manage and predict outcomes often left me anxious and restless. The teachings on swachhand, humility, and surrender have helped me see that my anxiety comes from self will and attachment to results, not from the situations themselves.

I have also started to reinforce the belief that there is a deeper stability within me that is not shaken by changing circumstances. Remembering that the soul is pure, peaceful, and beyond gain or loss helps me pause before reacting in worry or doubt. Instead of trying to control everything, I can now turn inward, remember the guidance of the Sadguru, and act calmly with faith. This shift is helping me trust life more, reduce overthinking, and face challenges with greater balance and clarity. Over time, this understanding is teaching me that peace is not something I must earn from the outside, but something I can rest in from within.

items.q: How do you personally recognise when pride is influencing your thoughts or actions?
a: I recognise pride influencing my thoughts or actions when I begin to feel an inner resistance toward correction or feedback. If someone points out a mistake and I immediately want to defend myself or prove that I was right, I know pride is active. It also appears as a quiet comparison with others, when I start measuring my worth by achievements, recognition, or being more capable than someone else. At times, pride hides behind helpfulness or competence, where I subtly expect appreciation or control how others see me.

Another clear sign is a loss of calmness. When pride takes over, my mind becomes tense, impatient, or easily hurt by small things. I notice that humility brings softness and understanding, while pride hardens my attitude. Through the teachings of Sri Atmasiddhi Shastra, especially verse 18, I have learned that pride is the most powerful obstacle because it blinds me to the truth and keeps me from surrendering to guidance. Recognising these patterns helps me pause, bow inwardly, and remind myself that the real goal is not to be right or superior, but to stay open, humble, and in harmony with the Guru’s intent.

items.q: What does humility look like in your daily life?
a: In my daily life, humility shows up in small but steady ways. It means being willing to listen instead of rushing to prove my point and accepting that I do not always know or need to control everything. When something goes wrong, humility helps me take responsibility instead of blaming others or the situation. It also means receiving feedback with openness and seeing it as an opportunity to grow rather than a personal attack.

Humility appears when I quietly remember that whatever I achieve, whether at work, in studies, or in relationships, is not entirely my doing but supported by many visible and invisible factors, including grace. It helps me stay calm in success and composed in failure, knowing that both are temporary. Most of all, humility means keeping my heart soft, respecting others’ perspectives, being kind even when I disagree, and staying grateful for the guidance of my Sadguru. In these ways, humility becomes a simple daily practice that replaces pride with peace and keeps me grounded in what truly matters.

items.q: How do you differentiate between knowledge that changes your life and knowledge that only fills your mind?
a: I differentiate between knowledge that changes my life and knowledge that only fills my mind by observing its effect on my thoughts and behaviour. When knowledge truly transforms me, it brings clarity, peace, and humility. It makes me more aware of my reactions and helps me live with greater calmness, compassion, and self control. This kind of knowledge simplifies my inner world and guides me toward right action. I feel lighter and more connected to my values after hearing or reflecting on it.

On the other hand, knowledge that only fills my mind stays at the level of information. It may sound impressive or increase my ability to talk about spiritual or worldly topics, but it does not change the way I live or think. It often feeds pride or comparison rather than peace. The study of Sri Atmasiddhi Shastra has helped me see that true knowledge is not measured by how much I know but by how deeply I apply it. Real knowledge moves from the head to the heart, leading to awareness and transformation, while mere words stay in the intellect and fade away without meaning.

parts.title: I. Answer in a few words.

items.q: Despite studying scriptures, which 3 aspects of inner work does the dry intellectualist miss out on due to which there is no inner transformation?
a: The dry intellectualist misses inner transformation because he neglects good conduct, becoming indifferent to humility and discipline. He also abandons the means of self-realisation, such as meditation, introspection, and repentance, leaving himself without any practical path. Finally, he fails in inner application, using the absolute viewpoint only in words without checking or changing his tendencies. Without these three, good conduct, sadhan, and inner application, scriptural study brings no inner change.

items.q: How has Pujyashri Ambalalbhai explained the virtue of Saralpanu (straightforwardness)?
a: Pujyashri Ambalalbhai explains saralpanu as the virtue of being straightforward in seeing and admitting one’s own faults. It means owning your mistakes without excuses, justifications, or emotional drama, and focusing honestly on the part you played rather than blaming others. A person with saralpanu is open, sincere, and willing to correct themselves quickly, creating the inner softness needed for spiritual growth.

items.q: How many verses has Shrimad Rajchandraji composed about kriyajada atmarthi?
a: Shrimad Rajchandraji has composed 5 verses about the kriyajada matarthi (mechanical ritualist)- Verses 24 to 28.

items.q: In this section, Shrimad Rajchandraji has described the kriyajada matarthi's beliefs regarding which three aspects?
a: Shrimad Rajchandraji describes the kriyajada matarthi’s false beliefs regarding three key aspects:
1. Guru (Verses 24 and 26)
2. God (Verse 25)
3. Dharma – scriptures, external attire, vows, and austerities (Verses 27 and 28)
So the three aspects are Guru, God, and Dharma.

items.q: Which two main characteristics of the inner state of the Lord are overlooked by a kriyajada?
a: A kriyajada overlooks the two main inner characteristics of the Lord:
1. Omniscience (sarvajnata)
2. Total non-attachment (vitaragata) He gets stuck in the outer glories and misses these true inner qualities.

parts.title: II. Identify and rectify the error in understanding in the statements below.

items.q: A person engaging in external vows, austerities etc. is a matarthi (bigot).
a: A person is not a matarthi merely because they engage in external vows and austerities. They become a matarthi only when they perform these practices with pride, show, or the desire for worldly respect, without understanding their inner purpose or observing their inner tendencies. External practices themselves are not wrong — the wrong inner attitude makes one a matarthi.

items.q: It is more beneficial to cherish your ego by reading more scriptures than by performing austerities like fasting.
a: Neither reading scriptures nor performing austerities is beneficial if the purpose is to cherish the ego. Spiritual progress comes only when scriptures and austerities are used to reduce pride and transform inner tendencies. If either is done to inflate the ego, both become obstacles. The benefit lies in humility and inner purification, not in the activity itself.

items.q: Jineshwar Bhagwan (Omniscient God) is worthy of worshipping because millions of celestial beings are at his service.
a: Jineshwar Bhagwan is not worthy of worship because of celestial beings, miracles, or external grandeur. These are merely karmic manifestations. The Lord is truly worthy of worship because of His inner state of omniscience and total non-attachment. It is these inner virtues—not celestial attendance—that define His greatness.

items.q: Shrimad Rajchandraji is against external renunciation in the name of inner renunciation.
a: Shrimad Rajchandraji is not against external renunciation. He only warns that external renunciation without inner renunciation is incomplete. External renunciation is valuable and meaningful when it reflects true inner detachment, but if the inner state remains filled with ego and passions, outer renunciation alone does not lead to spiritual progress.

items.q: Since engaging in spiritual practices can lead to ego, one should stop engaging in them.
a: One should not stop engaging in spiritual practices because they may give rise to ego. Instead, one should continue these practices with the right intention, using them to observe and reduce ego rather than avoid it. Spiritual practices are essential means for inner purification; the goal is to remove ego through them, not escape from them.

parts.title: III. Answer in one or two sentences.

items.q: Instead of just explaining the characteristics of a true seeker, why did Shrimad Rajchandraji also explain the characteristics of a bigot in so much detail?
a: Shrimad Rajchandraji explained the characteristics of a bigot in detail so that a seeker can identify and remove those faults within themselves. Without first recognizing what blocks spiritual progress, one cannot cultivate the qualities of a true seeker. This section serves as a mirror for self-reflection, preparing the mind for the path of liberation.

items.q: What is the subtle message given in verse 29:
a: The subtle message of Verse 29 is that merely understanding or speaking about the absolute viewpoint is not enough. If one neglects good conduct and abandons the practical means of self-purification, then even the highest philosophical knowledge becomes empty lip-adoption. Real spirituality requires living the truth through discipline, humility, and inner transformation, not just talking about it.

items.q: Which 2 criteria were given by Pujya Gurudevshri to check if we are reflecting on the scriptures correctly?
a: 1. Our passions should weaken. Correct reflection shows up as softer anger, reduced pride, less greed, and quicker recovery from emotional disturbances.

2. Our attachment to the world should start fading. Scriptural reflection is correct only if it leads to greater inner detachment, less fascination for worldly pleasures, and more inclination toward the Self. In short: Right reflection = weaker passions + growing inner detachment.

items.q: Why does a bigot feel more comfortable in the presence of asadguru?
a: A bigot feels more comfortable with an asadguru because the asadguru does not challenge or correct his ego. Instead, he offers praise, validation, and comfort, which allows the bigot’s pride to remain intact. In contrast, a Sadguru gives truth and honest correction, which pinches the ego, making the bigot uncomfortable and resistant.

items.q: Why is pride compared to sweet poison?
a: Pride is compared to sweet poison because it feels pleasant and satisfying in the moment, like sweetness, but it silently and gradually destroys spiritual progress, just as poison harms the body. Its danger lies in the fact that it appears enjoyable, making it harder to detect and remove, yet it is spiritually deadly.

parts.title: IV Self Reflection and Inner Inquiry:

items.q: Assess your own spiritual journey through the lens of the four virtues (subsidence of passions, inner detachment, straightforwardness, neutral attitude). Which of these do you find most challenging to cultivate, and what steps could you take to strengthen them in your daily life?
a: When I look at my journey through the four virtues, the one I find most challenging to cultivate is subsidence of passions. Even small situations can trigger irritation, hurt, or worry, and I notice how quickly my mind reacts. To strengthen this, I can practice a conscious pause before responding, use daily journaling to identify recurring triggers, and take a few minutes each day for stillness or breath awareness to soften my reactions.

I also want to deepen inner detachment, because I often get pulled outward by expectations, emotions, or what others may think. To support this, I can gently shift my focus from outcomes to intention and remind myself that real joy and stability come from within, not from external validation. Strengthening these two virtues forms a foundation for growing in straightforwardness and neutrality as well.

items.q: How has encountering the description of the matarthi (bigot) impacted your personal introspection?
a: Encountering the description of the matarthi has made my introspection much sharper and more honest. Instead of assuming I am progressing just because I do certain practices or know certain concepts, it has pushed me to examine my motives, reactions, and hidden ego more closely. It has helped me see where I may be doing things for image, comfort, or validation rather than true inner growth. This mirror has created a deeper longing to shift from outer activity to inner sincerity, and to cultivate the qualities of a true seeker with more humility and awareness.

items.q: Recall a moment when you acted harshly or impatiently with someone. Locate the mistakes in your behaviour, in the words you used, in the feelings behind them, and in the belief that supported them.
a: One moment that stands out is when I spoke impatiently to someone because I felt they weren’t meeting my expectations. Looking back, the mistake in my behaviour was reacting too quickly rather than pausing to understand their situation. The words I used were sharper than necessary, driven more by irritation than clarity. The feelings behind them were a mix of frustration, hurt, and the need to assert control. And underneath it all was a belief that things should happen according to my timing and my way, a subtle form of ego that made me feel justified in reacting harshly. Recognizing this helps me see how much gentleness and humility I still need to cultivate.

items.q: Think about a situation where you have resisted advice that challenged your pre-existing views. How will the guidance given in this section help you in such situations now?
a: I can think of situations where I resisted advice simply because it didn’t match the way I already saw things. At the time, I felt protective of my viewpoint and uncomfortable letting go of what felt familiar. The guidance in this section helps me see that this resistance usually comes from ego and insistence, not from clarity. It reminds me that when advice challenges me, it is often an opportunity to grow rather than a threat. Now, instead of defending my view immediately, I can pause, soften, and ask, “What truth might this person be seeing that I am missing?” This approach helps me stay more open, neutral, and willing to learn—qualities that move me closer to the mindset of a true seeker.

items.q: What would help you distinguish between genuine faith and blind attachment?
a: Genuine faith helps me grow inwardly, become calmer, and move closer to truth, while blind attachment keeps me stuck in comfort, habit, or emotional dependence. What would help me distinguish between the two is noticing the effect it has on my inner state: if my faith makes me more humble, open, and willing to examine myself, it is genuine; but if it makes me defensive, rigid, or afraid to question, it is attachment. Another helpful measure is checking whether I value inner qualities (virtue, purity, truth) over outer factors (family tradition, personality, appearances). The more I align with inner transformation rather than emotional loyalty, the more clearly I can see the difference between true faith and blind attachment.

parts.title: I. Answer in a few words (1 Mark Each)

items.q: According to an atmarthi, which attribute is a requisite for a Sadguru?
a: Self-realisation (Atmajnan) is the requisite attribute of a Sadguru according to an atmarthi.

items.q: What are the three faculties of a true seeker that act in unison when following a Sadguru's command?
a: Mind, speech, and body- the three faculties act in unison when following the Sadguru’s command.

items.q: At any given point in time, how many noble exterior practices can be helpful in attaining liberation?
a: Many- any number of noble exterior practices can be helpful if they inspire and lead toward the one path of liberation.

items.q: What is the only desire of a true seeker, with no other mental cravings?
a: Self-realisation- the true seeker has only this one desire and no other mental cravings.

items.q: What are the three constituents of the absolute path of liberation?
a: Right faith, right knowledge, and right conduct- the three jewels that constitute the absolute path of liberation.

parts.title: II. Correct my understanding

items.q: A true seeker rejects all Gurus of his family's tradition.
a: A true seeker does not reject family/sect Gurus out of disrespect. He respects everyone, but accepts only a Self-realised one as Sadguru for the purpose of liberation.

items.q: You meet a Sadguru (Jnani) through your self effort and you attain Self realisation (Atmajnan) through good karmic merits.
a: It is the opposite: Meeting a Sadguru (Jnani) happens because of strong past merits (puṇya). Attaining Self-realisation (atmajnan) happens through your present self-effort- surrender, worthiness, and following the Sadguru’s ajna.

items.q: Even without cultivating inner virtues, an individual can eventually take full advantage of a Sadguru's association due to past good merits.
a: Past merits can give you the association (yog) of a Sadguru, but without inner virtues (worthiness) you cannot benefit (jog) from that association. Param Krupalu Dev clearly states that until worthiness arises, one cannot take advantage of the Sadguru’s presence.

items.q: “Right thinking" (suvicharna) in the context of spiritual growth simply means having positive thoughts.
a: Right thinking” (suvicharna) does not mean general positive thinking. It means deep reflection, contemplation, discrimination, and meditation on the nature of the Self, arising from Sadguru’s teachings. It is the inner work that leads to Self-realisation.

items.q: The presentation of the six fundamental truths (shatpad) relies primarily on the seeker's existing faith and devotion, using the dialogue format to reinforce these beliefs through the recitation of sacred doctrines.
a: The six fundamental truths are not presented to reinforce the seeker’s existing faith or devotional feelings. Param Krupalu Dev introduces the shatpad to create right thinking and to give a clear, reasoned understanding of the path to liberation. The Guru–disciple dialogue format is used because it effectively resolves doubts, engages both heart and intellect, and makes the teachings practical and easy to grasp. Its purpose is to elevate the seeker’s understanding, not rely on what he already believes.

parts.title: III. Answer in few sentences.

items.q: What are the two supreme benefits of the association of a Living Sadguru mentioned by Pujya Gurudevshri?
a: Pujya Gurudevshri explains that the association of a Living Sadguru gives two supreme benefits: 1. All our doubts, confusions and inner curiosities about the path are gradually resolved in His presence. 2. Deep-rooted, otherwise uncontrollable faults and passions begin to drop away with comparatively little effort (“alp prayase jay”) under His guidance.

items.q: According to verse 41 - Jya pragte suvicharna, ... What is the initial outcome when right thinking emerges in a worthy seeker, and what is the ultimate outcome?"
a: According to Verse 41, when right thinking (suvicharna) arises in a worthy seeker, the initial outcome is the awakening of Self-knowledge / Self-realisation (nij jnan). The ultimate outcome is that through this knowledge, delusion is
destroyed, and the seeker ultimately attains the state of liberation (Nirvan).

items.q: What two purposes does Shrimad Rajchandraji mention in verse 42 for stating the six fundamental truths?
a: Shrimad Rajchandraji states two clear purposes for presenting the six fundamental truths (shatpad) in Verse 42: 1. To generate right thinking (suvicharna) in the seeker-the kind of thinking that turns the mind inward and prepares one for Self-realisation.
2. To give a correct understanding of the path of liberation (mokshmarg) — so the seeker clearly knows what to contemplate and what the true path consists of.

items.q: Instead of just saying that one who is not a matarthi is an atmarthi, why did Shrimad Rajchandraji compose one whole section for the traits of an atmarthi?
a: 1. A positive description inspires transformation. Saying “he is not a bigot” gives only a vague, negative definition. But describing the ātmārthī’s virtues, mindset, devotion, and purpose gives a clear, uplifting ideal for a seeker to grow toward. 2. It helps us cultivate and strengthen those virtues. By seeing each trait of an ātmārthī directly, we can identify what we already have and what we need to develop- something a negative definition can never provide.

items.q: Why is the path of liberation the same in all places and all times?
a: The path of liberation is the same in all places and all times because the nature of the soul is the same in all places and all times. Shrimad Rajchandraji explains in verse 36 that: 1.Liberation depends on the pure Self. 2. Since the soul does not change with region (kshetra), era (kal), or type of being (dravya). 3. The essential path leading to its realisation- right faith, right knowledge, and right conduct- must also remain unchanged universally.

parts.title: IV Reflective Questions

items.q: How might an aspirant in today's world discern a true Sadguru amidst various spiritual claims and what personal preparation would be essential before seeking such guidance?
a: In today’s world, where many spiritual figures make claims, an aspirant must rely on inner discrimination (vivek) rather than outer appeal. Shrimad Rajchandraji guides that a true Sadguru is identified not by robes, popularity, lineage, or oratory, but by Self-realisation- the one non-negotiable criterion. A Sadguru is one who is Self-realised, lives in equanimity, has unique awakening speech, and guides according to the seeker’s inner growth, not his preferences. Such a Guru knows both the truth and the seeker, and therefore becomes the right “key” to unlock the Self.

Before seeking or approaching such a Guru, the aspirant must first cultivate personal worthiness. This includes calming passions, developing sincerity, nurturing the desire for liberation, feeling the weariness of worldly wandering, and expanding compassion for all beings (verse 38). Additionally, the seeker must clarify why they want a Guru- not for peace, comfort, miracles, or social belonging, but for Self-realisation alone (“kaam ek atmarthnu, bijo nahi manrog”). With these virtues, the heart becomes receptive, and a true Sadguru naturally becomes recognizable and meaningful on the path.

items.q: Reflect on how your understanding of these verses could influence your approach to different spiritual traditions or practices you encounter, and what challenges might arise in maintaining a balance without insisting on your own method or criticizing others'.
a: Understanding these verses- especially the teaching that “the path of liberation is one in all three times, and whatever leads to it should be accepted or respected”- naturally softens my approach toward different spiritual traditions and practices. Instead of judging methods, I begin to look at their inner purpose: Do they reduce passions? Do they inspire detachment, compassion, or right thinking? If they genuinely help someone move toward purity and inner stillness, then, even if different from my own practice, they deserve respect. This perspective encourages humility, openness, and reverence for sincerity wherever it appears.

But maintaining this balance in real life is challenging. My mind may cling to methods that feel “right” or familiar and may subtly judge others’ practices as inferior or “less spiritual.” Personal preferences, ego-based certainty, or the comfort of tradition can make me insist on my own way. Recognizing this tendency, I must continuously return to the ātmārthī mindset: focus on my own inner transformation, avoid unnecessary comparison, and remember that liberation depends on inner purity, not external uniformity. The challenge is to remain rooted in my path without narrowing my vision, and to appreciate that many different practices can lead sincere seekers toward the same ultimate truth.

items.q: What conscious steps are you willing to take to elevate spiritual welfare from a mere interest to your exclusive, ultimate life's purpose, and what specific worldly desires or subtle mental cravings currently exist within me that might dilute this focus?
a: To make spiritual welfare my exclusive purpose, I am willing to create space each day for reflection, prioritize satsang over distraction, simplify my life, and approach the path with sincerity rather than seeking comfort or emotional support. I also want to consciously align my choices with the inner question, “Does this lead me closer to the Self?” At the same time, I recognize subtle cravings that dilute my focus: wanting validation, emotional security, control over situations, comfort, and approval from others. These small “man-rog” tendencies, preferences, attachments, and expectations, quietly pull me outward. By noticing them honestly and repeatedly redirecting my attention inward, I can strengthen my commitment to making ātmārth my true life purpose.

items.q: As you reflect on four virtues of a true seeker, which one do you find most challenging to cultivate in your daily life, and what specific internal and external steps could you initiate to strengthen it?
a: Among the four virtues, the one I find most challenging to cultivate is kashayni upshantta-the consistent calming of anger, pride, deceit, and greed in daily life. Even when I understand the teachings, small triggers, emotional reactions, expectations from others, or subtle ego-protective habits quickly re-activate these passions. They don’t always appear loudly, but often as irritation, defensiveness, comparison, or wanting things to go my way.

To strengthen this virtue, I can take internal steps such as pausing before reacting, honestly observing my triggers, journaling moments when kashay arises, and reminding myself that these reactions harm my own peace more than anyone else. Practicing forgiveness, humility, and detachment, even in small situations, can slowly weaken these tendencies.

Externally, I can create supportive conditions: reducing overstimulation, keeping my environment orderly, limiting exposure to people or situations that provoke unnecessary agitation, and staying close to satsang and noble company. By combining both inner awareness and outer discipline, I can gradually cultivate a calmer, softer, more receptive state that reflects the true seeker’s virtue.

items.q: Considering your current spiritual routine, how might you integrate a more comprehensive understanding of suvicharna (right thinking) into your daily life to foster deeper inner transformation beyond mere intellectual understanding?
a: To integrate a deeper understanding of suvicharna into my daily life, I need to move beyond just listening to teachings and actually let them shape my moment-to-moment thinking. This means consciously pausing throughout the day to recall Sadguru’s guidance, questioning the motives behind my actions, and shifting my thoughts from worldly preoccupations toward the nature of the Self. Instead of treating suvicharna as an occasional intellectual exercise, I can turn it into a living practice by reflecting after interactions, observing my reactions, and correcting them in real time.

I can also build small habits that keep right thinking active, like beginning and ending the day with contemplation, reviewing one teaching to apply for the day, and taking brief “awareness breaks” to recalibrate my focus. When I consistently engage with teachings through reflection, introspection, and application, suvicharna becomes less about understanding and more about inner transformation, gradually purifying my mind and preparing it for Self-realisation.

parts.title: I. Explain the disciple’s doubt. (2 Mark Each)

items.q: Why does the disciple believe in the existence of air even though he cannot see air, but does not believe in the existence of soul?
a: The disciple believes that air exists because even though it cannot be seen it can still be felt. For example we can feel air when the wind blows or when we breathe. Since air can be experienced by the senses he accepts that it exists.

The soul cannot be seen felt tasted smelled or heard. It cannot be experienced by any of the five senses. It is the knower of all five senses. I Because the disciple believes that only things experienced by the senses are real he does not believe in the existence of the soul

items.q: Why does the disciple think that the soul is another name for the breath?
a: The disciple thinks that the soul is the same as the breath because when breathing stops the body becomes lifeless. He observes that life continues as long as breath is present and ends when breath leaves the body. Because breath is clearly felt and experienced while the soul is not directly experienced by the senses the disciple assumes that breath itself is the soul. He believes there is no separate soul apart from the functioning breath.

items.q: Why does the disciple think that the soul is another name for the body itself?
a: The disciple thinks that the soul is another name for the body because all activities awareness and experiences are seen only as long as the body is alive. Since the body is directly visible and the soul is never experienced separately he believes that the body itself is what people call the soul

items.q: Why does the disciple think that the soul is another name for the senses?
a: The disciple thinks that the soul is another name for the senses because all knowing seeing hearing tasting smelling and touching happen through the sense organs. Since awareness functions only when the senses are active, the soul is not experienced separately and is the same.

items.q: Why does the disciple believe in the existence of pot, cloth etc. but not in the existence of the soul?
a: The disciple believes in the existence of pot cloth and other objects because they can be directly known by the senses. They can be seen touched and clearly experienced so their existence feels certain to him.

The soul cannot be seen or experienced by the senses in the same way. Since the disciple believes that only what is known through the senses is real he accepts pot and cloth but denies the existence of the soul

parts.title: II. Correct this understanding based on the learnings from Shri Atmasiddhi Shastra. (2 marks Each)

items.q: Even if you accept that knowingness is not an attribute of the body, senses etc., that does not prove the existence of the soul.
a: Knowingness cannot exist without a knower. If knowingness is not an attribute of the body, senses, or breath, then there must be a separate conscious entity in which knowingness resides. That conscious knower is what is called the soul. Therefore, accepting knowingness as independent of the body and senses does prove the existence of the soul, because an attribute cannot exist without its substance.

items.q: The brain, and not the soul coordinates the functions of the senses. Hence the soul does not exist.
a: The brain is only an instrument and cannot function independently. In a dead body the brain and senses are still present, yet no knowing or coordination takes place. This shows that coordination does not belong to the brain itself. The coordinating conscious principle is the soul, and the brain functions only in the presence of the soul. Therefore the soul does exist and is the real coordinator of the senses.

items.q: Feelings can be explained through the release of chemicals like oxytocin etc. in the body. They do not prove the existence of the soul.
a: Chemicals in the body are material and unconscious. They can explain physical changes in the body but they cannot explain awareness of feelings. Feelings such as happiness sorrow love or fear are known and experienced. Where there is knowing there must be a knower. Chemicals may support the experience but the conscious experiencer is the soul. Therefore feelings do point to the existence of the soul and cannot be explained by chemicals alone.

items.q: One cannot say that knowingness is an attribute of the soul, because there is no knowingness in the dream state and sleep state. Therefore the soul does not exist.
a: Knowingness does not disappear in dream or deep sleep. Even after waking up a person says I slept well or I had a dream. This shows that knowingness was present, because one later knows the experience of sleep or dream. The soul remains as continuous knowingness even when the senses and mind are inactive. Therefore knowingness is an attribute of the soul, and the soul does exist.

items.q: Not only the soul cannot be seen, but also none of its attributes can be seen. Hence the soul does not exist.
a: Not being seen does not mean not existing. Many real things cannot be seen directly but are known through their clear signs. The soul may not be seen, but its attribute of knowingness is constantly experienced as the feeling of I know and I am. This continuous awareness is the clear sign of the soul. Therefore, even though the soul and its attributes are not visible to the eyes, their existence is established through direct inner experience.

parts.title: III. Write the message of the examples below. (2 marks each)

items.q: A person inside a house uses a window as an instrument to see the hills outside.
a: Just as a person inside a house sees the hills outside through a window, the soul sees and knows the world through the senses. The window does not see by itself; it is only an instrument. In the same way, the senses do not know by themselves. The real seer and knower is the soul.

items.q: Individual departments in a business like production and marketing have limited functions, while a Head of Department (HOD) coordinates and knows the workings of all.
a: Each department in a business has its own limited function, just like each sense has its own specific role. The Head of Department knows and coordinates the work of all departments. In the same way, the senses work in limited areas, but there is one conscious entity that knows and coordinates all of them. That entity is the soul.

items.q: Electric gadgets are seen to function but the electricity that powers them is invisible.
a: Even though electric gadgets are seen working, the electricity that makes them function cannot be seen. Its existence is known from its effect. In the same way, the body and senses are seen to function, but the soul that gives them life and awareness is not visible. The existence of the soul is known through its effects, such as knowingness and consciousness.

items.q: A person with a lean body might possess supreme intelligence, whereas an elephant with a large body has much lesser intelligence.
a: This example shows that intelligence or knowingness does not depend on the size of the body. A lean human can have very high intelligence, while an elephant with a huge body has much less intelligence. Therefore knowingness is not an attribute of the body. It belongs to a separate conscious entity, which is the soul.

items.q: Hydrogen and oxygen can chemically react to form water, but water does not gain the property of consciousness. Also, hydrogen and oxygen remain distinct substances even when combined as water
a: This example shows that when two material substances combine, a new substance may form, but it does not gain consciousness. Hydrogen and oxygen together form water, yet water remains unconscious, and hydrogen and oxygen still remain distinct in nature. In the same way, when the soul and body are together, the body does not become conscious by itself, and the soul does not become the body. Both remain separate and distinct substances.

parts.title: IV. Answer in brief. (3 marks each)

items.q: How has Shrimad Rajchandraji woven the six fundamental truths in the first verse of Shri Atmasiddhi Shastra: Je swaroop samjya vina, pamyo dukh anant; Samjavyu te pad namu, Shri Sadguru Bhagwant.
a: The line “Je swaroop samjya vina, pamyo dukh anant” shows that ignorance of the true nature of the soul is the cause of endless suffering, which implies that the soul exists, is eternal, is the doer and receiver of karma, and therefore undergoes bondage and suffering.

The line “Samjavyu te pad namu, Shri Sadguru Bhagwant” shows that there exists a path to liberation, and that this path is taught by a true Sadguru. This implies that liberation exists and that there is a right means to attain it.

Thus, in one verse, Shrimad Rajchandraji establishes the existence of the soul, its bondage through ignorance, the possibility of liberation, and the presence of a true path taught by the Sadguru, thereby beautifully encompassing all six fundamental truths.

items.q: Write any three reasons the disciple of Shri Atmasiddhi Shastra a sushishya - an ideal disciple.
a: The disciple of Shri Atmasiddhi Shastra is a sushishya or ideal disciple for the following reasons.

First he is an atmarthi who genuinely seeks Self realisation and is not interested in worldly gains like wealth or fame. Second even while having doubts he has deep faith and respect for the Sadguru and believes that only the Sadguru can resolve his confusion. Third he presents his doubts with humility and sincerity and asks for clarification to correct his own understanding rather than to argue or prove the Guru wrong.

items.q: What are the two main reasons for our false identification with the body? In relation to this, why has Shrimad Rajchandraji repeated three parts of verse 49 in verse 50?
a: The two main reasons for our false identification with the body are ignorance of the true nature of the soul and constant close association of the soul with the body. Because the soul and body remain together for a long time and the soul lacks Self realisation, the habit develops of thinking I am the body.

Shrimad Rajchandraji repeats the key parts of verse 49 in verse 50 to firmly break this deep rooted habit. Since body identification is very strong and old, he repeats the teaching using an example so that the distinction between soul and body becomes clear not only intellectually but also firmly settles in understanding.

items.q: Write any three points explaining the aptness of the example of sword and sheath given in verse 50.
a: The example of sword and sheath is apt for explaining the relationship between the soul and the body for the following reasons.

First the sword and the sheath remain very close and are always found together yet they are clearly separate and different, just like the soul and the body. Second the sheath only covers the sword but does not become the sword. In the same way the body only covers the soul but does not become the soul. Third the properties of the sword and sheath are completely different. The sword is sharp and  functional while the sheath is inert. Similarly the soul is conscious while the body is unconscious.

items.q: Give any six reasons why an object cannot be seen even if it exists.
a: First it may be too far away to be seen by the eyes. Second it may be too close to the eyes to be seen clearly. Third it may be behind the observer and therefore outside the field of vision. Fourth it may be covered or hidden by something else. Fifth there may be no light or insufficient light to see it. Sixth it may be too small to be seen with the naked eyes.

parts.title: V. Reflective Questions (3 marks each)

items.q: Consider the questions that occupy your mind daily. What does the nature of your dominant questions reveal about your current priorities as a seeker, and how might you consciously shift your focus toward the questions of the Self?
a: The questions that occupy my mind daily reveal where my attention and priorities lie. When most of my questions are about health career relationships or external situations it shows that my focus is still mainly outward and worldly. This indicates that my concern is more about comfort security and control rather than understanding the Self.

To shift toward questions of the Self I can consciously pause and observe who is the one experiencing these worries and thoughts. By asking questions like who am I who is aware of this thought or what remains constant while situations change I can slowly turn my attention from the outer world to the inner knower and move forward as a seeker.

items.q: In your spiritual discussions or when facing personal doubts, do you tend to argue to prove a point, or do you approach the situation with the humility and openness to truly receive a satisfactory solution, even if it contradicts your current understanding?
a: When facing spiritual discussions or personal doubts I often notice a tendency to protect my current understanding or justify my point of view. This shows subtle attachment to ego and ideas rather than pure truth seeking.

With reflection I see the importance of humility and openness shown by the disciple of Shri Atmasiddhi Shastra. By consciously approaching doubts with the attitude that the limitation may be in my understanding and not in the teaching I become more receptive. This openness allows true solutions to be received even when they challenge my existing beliefs and helps me progress on the path of Self realisation.

items.q: Reflect on your daily fears, desires, and attachments. How do your reactions to physical appearance, health, comfort, and aging reveal the true depth of your body-identification, and what is one small, conscious step you can take to begin living from a more soul-centric identity?
a: My daily fears, desires and attachments clearly show how strongly I still identify with the body. Worries about physical appearance, health, comfort and aging reveal that I often equate my sense of self with how the body looks, feels or performs. When these aspects are threatened anxiety and resistance arise which shows that body identification still runs deep.

One small conscious step I can take is to regularly pause and observe these reactions and remind myself that I am the knower of these experiences, not the body experiencing them. By gently shifting attention from the changing body to the steady awareness that notices these changes I can begin living from a more soul centric identity.

items.q: When you recognize moments of misery in your life, how deeply do you trace their root cause back to the absence of spiritual knowledge?
a: When I recognize moments of misery in my life and reflect deeply I see that their root cause is often the absence of spiritual knowledge. When I forget my true nature as the soul I identify with the body thoughts and emotions and expect lasting happiness from temporary things. This false identification leads to fear, attachment and disappointment which then turn into misery.

As my awareness grows I am able to trace suffering back to ignorance of the Self rather than external situations. This understanding helps me shift from blaming circumstances to recognizing the need for deeper self understanding and spiritual clarity.

items.q: Throughout your day, your attention is constantly focused on the objects of knowledge - sights, sounds, thoughts, and emotions. How can you practice shifting your focus from the 'known' to the silent, ever-present 'knower' within, transforming everyday activities into moments of self-awareness?
a: Throughout the day my attention naturally goes to sights, sounds, thoughts and emotions because this habit has been practiced for a long time. To shift from the known to the knower I can gently pause during ordinary activities and notice the awareness that is already present and knowing these experiences. Instead of following the object I can rest for a moment in the simple sense of I am the one who is aware.

By practicing this during simple moments such as walking, eating or listening I can slowly transform daily activities into moments of self awareness. This repeated turning inward helps weaken attachment to objects and strengthens awareness of the silent ever present knower within.

parts.title: I. Answer in one or two Sentences (2 Mark Each)

items.q: What is the homework given to the disciple in verse 70? (Kyare koi vastuno, keval hoi na nash; Chetan pamey nash toh, kema bhaley tapas.)
a: In Verse 70, the Guru asks the disciple to think carefully and find out what the soul turns into if it is truly destroyed, because nothing is ever completely wiped out. If consciousness really ends, the disciple must show what it changes into, and not just assume it disappears.

items.q: What are the two meanings of "deh matra sanyog chhe". “Deh
a: matra sanyog chhe” has two meanings: first, the body is only a combination of non-living elements; second, the body is merely in a temporary association with the soul.

items.q: Why can't the soul merge into something else when destroyed, or just vanish into nothing?
a: The soul cannot merge into something else or vanish into nothing because no substance is ever completely destroyed; it can only change form. Since consciousness cannot turn into non-conscious matter, it cannot simply disappear or dissolve into something else.

items.q: Explain how the Guru uses the point of speaking to prove that the soul is not "only momentary".
a: The Guru explains that to know and speak about momentariness, the knower must exist for more than one moment. Since speaking requires continuity over at least two moments, the soul cannot be “only momentary.”

parts.title: II. Correct my understanding (2 marks Each)

items.q: There is no need to believe in transmigration of the soul to explain variations in tendencies of anger etc. Science can explain it through genes, sociology can explain it through the environment in which the person was brought up.
a: This understanding is incomplete because genes and environment do not fully explain why strong tendencies appear from birth, even before training or experience. The Guru explains that such variations point to past-life impressions (sanskar), which science and environment alone cannot account for.

items.q: Substances like pot, cloth etc. exist only for a limited period of time. Soul too is a substance - so it too exists only for a limited period of time.
a: This conclusion is incorrect because pot and cloth are destroyed only in their form, not as substances- their matter continues in a different form. Similarly, the soul, though a substance, does not cease to exist; only its states change, so it is not limited in existence.

items.q: The soul, having the attribute of knowingness, can know about its own creation and destruction.
a: This is incorrect because to know creation, the knower must exist before creation, and to know destruction, the knower must exist after destruction. The soul cannot know its own creation or destruction, since that would require it to exist before and after itself, which is logically impossible.

items.q: It is possible for substances to change forms - this means the soul can change into matter and vice-versa.
a: This is incorrect because changing form does not mean changing substance. The Guru explains that matter and soul are two distinct substances, and while their states may change, consciousness cannot turn into matter, nor can matter turn into consciousness.

parts.title: III. Answer in Brief (3 marks each)

items.q: Why does the disciple feel that the soul is created and gets destroyed along with the birth and death of the body? Why does he feel that the soul is momentary?
a: The disciple feels that the soul is created and destroyed with the body because he observes consciousness only in a living body and observes that it is not there anymore when the body dies. He also feels the soul is momentary because thoughts, emotions, and experiences change continuously, leading him to believe that the knower itself changes and is destroyed at every moment.

items.q: Explain the example of three stages given by Shrimad Rajchandraji in verse 68 to explain that the soul is not momentary.
a: Shrimad Rajchandraji explains that a person passes through three stages of childhood, youth, and old age, while the body and states keep changing. Even though these stages are different, the same knower experiences all of them, showing that the soul remains continuous and is not momentary.

items.q: Explain the example of intoxication usually given to support the argument of creation of consciousness from non-conscious matter. How would you refute this?
a: The intoxication example says that grapes and water are not intoxicating on their own, but when combined and fermented they produce wine, so consciousness can similarly arise from non-conscious matter. This is refuted by pointing out that intoxication already exists in a latent form in grapes and is merely manifested by fermentation, whereas non-conscious matter has no trace of knowingness, so consciousness cannot arise from it.

items.q: Explain the scientific method used by Shrimad Rajchandraji in verse 67. What is the observation, inference and conclusion mentioned in this verse? (Krodhadi tartamyata sarpadikni may, Poorvajanma sanskar te, jeev nityata tyay.)
a: In Verse 67, Shrimad Rajchandraji uses inference based on observation. The observation is that living beings show different degrees of tendencies like anger, fear, or instinct from birth, even without learning. From this, he infers that these tendencies come from past-life impressions (sanskar), and concludes that since the soul existed before this birth, it is eternal (nitya).

parts.title: IV. Reflective Questions (3 marks each)

items.q: Reflect on a moment when you experienced strong agitation or misery; examining that emotional state now, how does applying the rule (the knower must be separate from and survive the known) help you detach from defining your essential identity based on that transient feeling?
a: After I lost my job, the sadness and regret didn’t go away quickly. For almost three months, and even sometimes now, I keep thinking about what happened and wishing things had gone differently. At that time, it felt like this pain was who I was.

But when I look at it using the idea that the one who knows is separate from what is felt, things become clearer. During those months, I was able to notice my anxiety, feel the regret, and later think back on those moments. That means there was always a part of me that was watching these feelings. The emotions kept coming and going, but the one who noticed them stayed the same.

Understanding this helps me see that the job loss and the emotions around it are experiences I went through, not my true identity. Even if the feelings lasted a long time, they were still temporary, and they do not define who I really am.

items.q: Where do you frequently assign "doership" or creation in your life (e.g., career achievements, raising children, personal habits)? By accepting the principle that external manifestation is merely a change in form, how can you reduce the ego and anxiety tied to the perceived failure or success of these creations?
a: I often assign doership not only to big things like my career, but also to small daily actions, such as creating a to-do list and trying to “complete” my day. I start believing that finishing tasks is something I must fully control. When I do not complete a task properly or stay present while doing it, I feel frustrated or disappointed, as if I failed at the moment itself. Many times, my focus shifts from doing the task sincerely to just crossing it off the checklist. By accepting that external outcomes are only changes in form, I can see that completing or not completing a task does not define my value. The checklist is just a tool, not something I am creating or owning as part of my identity. What matters more is the intention and awareness with which I act in the present moment. This understanding reduces ego when I “succeed” and lowers anxiety when I “fail,” helping me approach daily actions with more calm, balance, and honesty.

items.q: Observe a tangible sign of physical change in yourself (e.g., changes in energy, appearance, or strength). Instead of identifying with the decaying form, how can you intentionally focus on the still centre that witnesses this process?
a: I notice physical changes in my body, such as having less energy on some days and not feeling as strong or active as I once did. I feel lethargic and negative at times. Sometimes my appearance seems to change, and this makes me feel worried or uncomfortable with my own body. It is easy to start believing that these changes mean something is wrong with me.

When I look more carefully, I realize that there is a quiet part of me that notices these changes. My energy rises and falls, and my body keeps changing, but the awareness that observes this process remains steady. By gently bringing my attention to this observing presence instead of the changing body, I remind myself that I am not the decaying form. I am the one who is aware of it. This helps me stay grounded and peaceful even as physical changes continue.

items.q: What deeply held beliefs or assumptions do you maintain about the spiritual path (or reality itself) that might be fundamentally illogical or internally inconsistent, and how do you intend to subject these to rigorous testing or contemplation for resolution?
a: One deeply held belief I notice in myself is the idea that if I am on the right spiritual path, I should feel peaceful, focused, and emotionally stable most of the time. When I experience anxiety, regret, confusion, or repeated emotional struggles, I often assume that I am failing spiritually or not practicing correctly. At the same time, I also believe that spiritual growth is meant to remove suffering and bring clarity. Holding both of these ideas together creates an inner contradiction, because real life shows me that growth often comes with discomfort, self-doubt, and emotional upheaval.

I also notice that sometimes I expect understanding to come quickly, as if that insight should appear suddenly and stay with me permanently once I say yes I understand something. When my old patterns return almost everyday, I judge myself harshly, go into a negative mindset, and forget that habits and conditioning develop over a long time and do not disappear instantly. This expectation is illogical because it ignores how change actually happens.

To resolve these inconsistencies, I intend to test my beliefs through honest observation rather than blind expectation. Instead of assuming that discomfort means failure, I will observe whether difficult emotions actually reveal deeper attachments and false identifications. I plan to reflect regularly on my reactions, compare my assumptions with reason and experience, and allow questioning rather than rushing toward conclusions. Through this process of careful contemplation and self-inquiry, I hope to replace rigid beliefs with clearer understanding and a more stable, grounded approach to the spiritual path.

parts.title: I. Answer in one or two Sentences (2 Mark Each)

items.q: Explain the disciple's doubt - Karma jeevno dharma. How does the Guru resolve this doubt?
a: The disciple doubts that Karma jeevno dharma means the bondage of karma is the inherent nature of the soul, implying it can never be eliminated and liberation is impossible. The Guru resolves this by explaining that karmic bondage occurs only if the soul engages in impure activity; hence it is neither automatic nor the soul’s true nature, but a removable tendency.

items.q: What does the disciple mean when he says: "ka nahi, ka nahi jaay"?
a: By saying ka nahi, ka nahi jaay, the disciple means that either the soul is not the doer of karma at all, or if it is the doer, that doership can never be removed. Thus, he concludes that liberation has no real purpose because karmic doership would either not belong to the soul or would remain forever.

items.q: Which of the five doubts of the disciple regarding doership of dravya karma are influenced by the Charvak philosophy? Why?
a: The second doubt- that karmas bind automatically (sahaj swabhav) without any conscious cause, is influenced by Charvak philosophy, because Charvak accepts only matter and chance, denying soul, consciousness, and moral causation. Hence, karma is seen as accidental and purposeless, with no role of conscious doership.

items.q: Which partial truth is the disciple considering as the complete truth, due to which he is feeling that the soul cannot be the doer of karmas? Actually, from which viewpoint is it true?
a: The disciple is taking the partial truth that the soul is pure, unattached (asang), and non-doer as the complete truth, and therefore concludes that the soul cannot be the doer of karmas. This is actually true only from the absolute (nishchay) viewpoint, whereas from the practical (vyavahar) viewpoint the soul, due to impure engagement, is indeed the doer of karmic bondage

parts.title: II. Give reasons for the following. (2 marks Each)

items.q: If God is not the doer of karmas, then why should one worship God?
a: Even though God is not the doer of karmas, one worships God because God represents the soul in its pure, perfected state, free from all karmas. Worship is done to develop devotion, inspiration, and the aspiration to attain the same pure state, not to seek intervention in karmic actions.

items.q: If karmas are matter, and matter has form - then why can't karmas be seen by us?
a: Although karmas are material, they are composed of extremely subtle (suksma) matter, far finer than gross physical particles. Due to this extreme subtlety, karmas are beyond the range of our sense organs and instruments, and therefore cannot be seen.

items.q: If karmas get bound automatically, then why would liberation be pointless?
a: If karmas were to bind automatically, without the soul’s conscious involvement, then the soul would have no control over bondage or release. In that case, even after liberation karmas could keep binding again, making effort meaningless and liberation impossible.

items.q: Why do objects like pot, cloth etc. not acquire karma?
a: Objects like pots or cloth do not acquire karma because they are inanimate (jada) and lack consciousness, which is essential for inspiring karmic bondage. Only a sentient soul, through conscious engagement such as attachment or aversion, can bind karmas.

parts.title: III. Answer in Brief (3 marks each)

items.q: Explain the disciple's doubt - Karma j karta karma. How does the Guru resolve this doubt?
a: The disciple doubts that karma j karta karma means karmas themselves give rise to new karmas, making the soul a mere witness and not the doer. The Guru resolves this by explaining that inanimate karma has no power to inspire or initiate action; without conscious inspiration (chetan prerna) from the soul, karmic bondage cannot occur. Thus, the soul, through its inner engagement, is established as the true doer of karmas.

items.q: Mention any 4 questions that would arise if we were to accept God as the prompter or doer of karmas.
a: If God were accepted as the prompter or doer of karmas, the following questions would arise:
1. Why should the soul be held responsible for good or bad actions if God inspires them?
2. Why would a perfect and pure God inspire sinful or cruel actions?
3. On what basis would God distribute different joys and sufferings among souls?
4. What would be the meaning or need of effort, restraint, or spiritual practice by the soul?

items.q: Who built the Ashram? Using this example, explain what the soul is a doer of, from the absolute and relative viewpoints.
a: From the relative (vyavahar) viewpoint, we say that a person built the Ashram, because the soul is the instrumental doer through intention and effort. From the absolute (nishchay) viewpoint, the soul does not create external objects; it is the doer only of its own inner states (bhava), while matter itself transforms into forms like buildings.

items.q: With the example of hot and cool water, explain the nature of the soul and why the soul acquires karmas.
