a: Just as water is neither hot nor cold by nature but becomes so due to contact with fire or ice, the soul is pure and non-attached by nature. The soul acquires karmas not because it is impure by nature, but because due to ignorance and inner reactions (attachment–aversion) it comes into association with karmic matter, leading to bondage.

parts.title: IV. Reflective Questions (3 marks each)

items.q: Do I rigorously think through multiple alternatives and attempt to derive a conclusion before posing fundamental questions, or do I rush to queries and retreat into frustration when faced with difficulty?
a: I try to slow down and really think before I ask big questions, instead of just reacting right away. I look at different possibilities, try to understand them, and see if they make sense. When things get confusing or difficult, I sometimes feel stuck, but I remind myself that struggle is normal. Instead of getting upset or giving up, I try to stay calm, reflect again, and keep learning, even if it takes time.

items.q: How consciously and frequently do I rely on doctrines like "God's will" (Hari Ichha) as an intellectual shield, thereby avoiding personal responsibility and facing the consequences of my own actions?
a: I notice that many times it feels easier to say this is God’s will (Hari Ichha) because it gives instant comfort and reduces mental stress. However, when I look deeper, I realize that I sometimes use this idea as a shield to avoid taking responsibility for my own thoughts, reactions, and actions. By doing so, I may escape guilt or fear in the moment, but I also miss the opportunity to learn, improve, and grow spiritually. Becoming more conscious of this habit helps me pause, reflect on my own role in the situation, and accept that my choices and inner responses shape my experiences and their consequences.

items.q: How often does my daily participation in traditionally auspicious activities transition into awareness of my pure self, rather than remaining mere good karmas which still lead to rebirth?
a: I often need to examine whether my daily involvement in auspicious activities, such as prayers, rituals, charity, or spiritual study, is truly helping me connect with awareness of my pure Self. Many times, these actions are done out of habit, social tradition, fear, or desire for good results, and therefore remain limited to producing good karmas that still bind me to rebirth. Only when I perform these activities with inner awareness, detachment, and the intent to observe my thoughts and reactions do they become a means for spiritual growth. This reflection reminds me that external goodness alone is not enough; without self-awareness, even virtuous actions cannot lead to liberation.

items.q: In moments when past karmas are fructifying as favourable or unfavourable situations, do I exercise the conscious choice to remain equanimous, or do I modify myself into likes-dislikes, thereby initiating new bondage?
a: When pleasant or unpleasant situations arise due to my past karmas, I need to observe how I respond internally. Many times, instead of remaining calm and balanced, I allow myself to slip into liking pleasant situations and disliking painful ones, reacting with attachment or aversion. In those moments, I unknowingly create new bondage by identifying with emotions rather than staying as a witness. This reflection reminds me that while I cannot control the arrival of situations, I always have the conscious choice to respond with equanimity, and that choice alone decides whether old karmas end or new ones begin.

parts.title: I. Answer in one Sentences (2 Mark Each)

items.q: Mention any two differences seen among individuals from birth that indicate these effects cannot exist without a cause.
a: The fact that one person is born a pauper (raank) and another a king (nrup) shows clear differences from birth that cannot exist without a cause.
Differences seen at birth such as being born healthy or sick, intelligent or dull, or into a wealthy or poor family indicate effects that must arise from prior causes (past karmas).

items.q: What are the names of the 4 gatis (types of forms a soul can take)?
a: Dev gati- Celestial (heavenly beings), Narki gati- Hellish beings, Manushya gati-Human beings, Tiryanch gati- Animals and other sub-human forms.

items.q: What four attributes get fixed for karmic particles at the time they bind with the soul?
a: Prakriti Bandh- Type or nature of karma (what kind of karma it becomes). Sthiti Bandh- Duration (how long the karma will remain bound). Anubhag Bandh- Intensity (how strongly it will give its result). Pradesh Bandh- Quantity (how many karmic particles bind).

items.q: Material karmas naturally fall off once their results have been experienced. Then why does the worldly soul never experience even a single moment free from karmic influence?
a: Material karmas do shed after giving their fruits, but the worldly soul never experiences even a single moment free from karmic influence because, at the time of experiencing (uday), it creates new impure feelings (bhaavkarma), which immediately bind fresh karmic particles, thus continuing the endless cycle of bondage.

items.q: On earth itself, there are places and situations that cause beings pain or give them comfort. Why, then, is there a need for realms like heaven and hell to experience the fruits of karmas?
a: Even though we experience happiness and suffering on earth, some karmas are so powerful that their full results cannot be experienced here, so special realms like heaven and hell exist, by the natural law of karma, to allow those intense results to be fully experienced.

parts.title: II. Answer in brief (3 Marks Each)

items.q: Explain the doubt in the disciple's mind regarding karmas being the inflicter of the karmic fruits.
a: The disciple’s doubt is that karmas are inanimate (jada) and have no consciousness or knowingness, so they cannot decide what fruit to give, when to give it, to whom to give it, and in what intensity. Since giving fruits appears to require intelligence and planning, he questions how lifeless karmic particles could “inflict” results on the soul, and therefore doubts whether the soul can truly be called the receiver of karmic fruits

items.q: According to the disciple, what problem arises if we accept God as the giver of the fruits of karmas? What problem arises if we don't accept Him as the fruit giver?
a: If we accept God as the giver of the fruits of karmas, then although it becomes easy to establish that the soul is the receiver, God’s Godliness is compromised, because He would have to act like a worldly administrator dispensing rewards and punishments.

If we do not accept God as the fruit-giver, then the disciple feels that world order (jagat niyam) and designated places like heaven and hell for experiencing karmic fruits cannot exist, leading to confusion about how karmic results are delivered

items.q: Dogs - luxurious life - owner. Write the example in brief and explain its message.
a: In the example, the Guru describes how some dogs live in huge mansions, eat special food, are taken on car rides, and are cared for by helpers, while their owners, though wealthy, are stressed, overworked, and have no time to rest.

The message is that worldly fortune and comfort are not always where we assume them to be; such differences in pleasure and suffering are the results of one’s own past karmas, and each soul experiences the fruits it has itself bound

items.q: If God is the giver of fruits of karmas, why can He not be just and compassionate at the same time?
a: If God is the giver of fruits of karmas, then to be just, He must strictly punish wrong actions and reward good ones according to law; but to be compassionate, He would have to forgive or reduce punishments. Thus, if He shows justice, compassion seems compromised, and if He shows compassion, justice seems compromised, so He cannot be perfectly just and perfectly compassionate at the same time in this role.

items.q: What example does the Guru give to resolve the first doubt of the disciple?
a: To resolve the first doubt (that lifeless karma cannot give fruits), the Guru gives the example of poison and nectar, they do not know their own effects, yet the person who consumes them experiences the result. Similarly, karmic matter may be insentient, but it still gives its results, and the soul experiences them.

items.q: What key insight is the disciple missing, due to which the Guru explains the process of karmic bondage first? Explain the process of karmic bondage.
a: Key insight the disciple is missing: The disciple is only thinking of dravya karma (material, lifeless karmas) and forgetting bhaavkarma (impure feelings of the soul); he does not understand that karmas are first “programmed” at the time of bondage through conscious impure feelings

Process of karmic bondage: When impure feelings such as anger, attachment, or desires arise within the soul (bhaavkarma), they activate the soul’s energy and attract karmic particles (karman vargana). These particles then bind to the soul as dravya karma, and at that time their type, duration, intensity, and quantity are fixed.

parts.title: III. Reflective Questions (3 marks each)

items.q: Do you harbor an unconscious desire for God to be compassionate and forgiving when you are wrong, and to be strictly just when others wrong you? Do you recognise that this fluctuating expectation contradicts the metaphysical reality of a perfectly impartial Supreme Being?
a: Yes, when I honestly reflect on myself, I notice that I often want God to be compassionate and forgiving when I make mistakes, but strictly just when someone wrongs me. When I suffer, I feel that justice must be served; when I am at fault, I quietly hope for mercy.

I can see that this expectation is self-centered and inconsistent. If God is truly a perfectly impartial and pure Supreme Being, He cannot shift between justice and compassion based on my personal convenience. Recognising this helps me understand that my fluctuating expectations come from my own attachments and not from the nature of a truly impartial reality.

items.q: Think of a major disparity or injustice you observed in the world (or felt personally), which led you to believe the situation was unjustifiable or discriminatory. Did you dedicate energy to blaming external entities or fate for these effects? Did you struggle with the question "Why me?" How does understanding the law of causation shift your emotional stance from feeling victimized to accepting absolute responsibility for the consequences that arrive?
a: When I think about a big unfair situation I saw or experienced, I remember feeling that it was not right. I did spend time blaming other people, circumstances, or even fate. The question: Why me? came up in my mind, and it made me feel hurt and frustrated.

But when I understand the law of cause and effect, that nothing happens without a reason, my thinking slowly changes. Instead of feeling like a victim, I begin to see that my present situation may be the result of past causes, even if I do not clearly remember them.

This understanding reduces my anger and blame. The question “Why me?” slowly changes to “There must be a reason.” I feel more responsible for my reactions and future actions. Instead of feeling helpless, I feel calmer and more accepting.

items.q: Consider a major achievement in the material world (e.g., acquiring wealth, a degree, or winning a competition). Did you go into a feeling of ego, crediting yourself for the results? How will you apply your understanding of these verses to cultivate dispassion and humility?
a: When I achieved something important, like earning a degree, gaining success, or reaching a goal, I felt pride and a sense of: I did this.I credited myself for the hard work and results, and ego quietly entered my mind. But after understanding these verses, I realize that achievements are not only the result of present effort; they are also the fruition of past karmas. Many unseen causes, circumstances, abilities, opportunities, support from others, all play a role. Recognizing this helps reduce ego. Instead of thinking, “I alone achieved this,” I can think, “This is a result of many causes coming together.” This understanding helps me cultivate humility and dispassion. I can still work sincerely, but without excessive pride. Success becomes something to accept calmly, not something to cling to. It reminds me that just as success comes due to causes, it can also pass, so staying balanced is wiser than becoming arrogant.

items.q: Recall a time when carelessness, laziness or distraction led to a mistake, conflict, or harm, which you dismissed as an unintentional error (e.g., forgetting an important date, breaking something, speaking thoughtlessly). Did you believe that because your intent was not malicious, the action carried no spiritual consequence? How does the understanding of these verses change your standard for diligence and awareness?
a: I can recall times when I was careless, distracted, or lazy and made a mistake, like forgetting something important or speaking without thinking. At that moment, I comforted myself by saying, I didn’t mean it, and believed that since my intention was not bad, it would not carry any real spiritual consequence. But these verses teach that even carelessness (pramad) and lack of awareness are forms of impurity, and that actions of mind, speech, and body still create effects, even if there was no malicious intent. Understanding this raises my standard of responsibility. It reminds me that spiritual life is not only about avoiding obvious wrongdoing, but also about being alert, careful, and conscious in every moment. Now I see that awareness itself is important. Instead of excusing mistakes as “unintentional,” I try to be more mindful and attentive. This understanding encourages greater diligence, sincerity, and inner discipline in my daily life.

parts.title: I. Answer in one Sentences (2 Mark Each)

items.q: In the third and fourth fundamental truths, the Guru established the principle that each activity is fruitful. In that context, what principle is established here using the words 'tem nivrutti safalta'?
a: Using the words “tem nivrutti safalta” the Guru establishes that just as engagement in shubh-ashubh karmas is fruitful, cessation (nivrutti) from them is also fruitful, and its result is liberation (moksh).

items.q: Which cycle regarding karma does the disciple believe to be endless?
a: The disciple believes the cycle of acquiring karmas, experiencing their fruits, reacting with likes-dislikes, and thereby binding new karmas again to be endless.

items.q: 'Dehadik sanyogno atyantik viyog' - using these words, explain the similarity and difference between death and liberation.
a: Both death and liberation involve separation from the body, but death is only temporary separation with re-association (new body), whereas “dehadik sanyogno atyantik viyog” in liberation means permanent separation from body and karmas with no return.

items.q: Explain the characteristics of liberation described in verse 91 - liberation from outer and inner viewpoints.
a: Liberation is described as inner freedom from shubhashubh feelings (no likes-dislikes) and outer freedom as permanent disassociation from body, karmas, and all material associations, resulting in infinite bliss.

parts.title: II. Answer in brief (3 Marks Each)

items.q: What commonly prevailing belief in religious societies about auspicious and inauspicious karmas is negated subtly through the disciple's doubt in verse 88 (karma rahit na kyay)? Explain why this belief is not true.
a: The commonly prevailing belief is that auspicious karmas (punya) lead to liberation while only inauspicious karmas (paap) cause bondage, but this is not true because both shubh and ashubh karmas bind the soul. Punya leads to pleasant experiences (like heaven) and paap to suffering (like hell), yet neither results in a karmaless state, and liberation is attained only by going beyond and destroying both.

items.q: Explain the disciple's second doubt regarding the existence of the state of liberation presented in verse 88. ‘Shubh karey fal bhogve, devadi gatimai; Ashubh karey narkadi fal, karma rahit na kyai.’ How does the Guru resolve this doubt?
a: The disciple doubts liberation by observing that shubh karmas lead to heavenly experiences and ashubh karmas to hellish experiences, yet in all four gatis the soul is always associated with karmas (karma rahit na kyai), so a karmaless state seems impossible. The Guru explains that the disciple has only observed the results of engagement (shubhashubh) but not cessation (nivrutti), and just as engagement is proven to be fruitful, withdrawal from shubh-ashubh is also valid. This connects to samvar (stoppage of new karmas) and nirjara (shedding of old karmas), resulting in a truly karmaless state (moksh) that exists beyond the four gatis.

parts.title: III. Reflective Questions (3 marks each)

items.q: Reflect on an auspicious activity (like charity, ritual, or devotion) you perform: Are you engaging in it primarily with awareness, or are you feeling satisfied that it will lead to liberation?
a: When I reflect on my actions, I realize that I often pray and do rituals with the hope that something good will happen, like doing well in an interview. This shows that I am still focused on getting results from my actions. I feel that if I pray more, I will get a better outcome. According to the teaching, these actions can bring good results and comfort, but they do not lead to liberation. Liberation comes when I perform these actions without expecting anything in return, and when I stay calm, aware, and steady inside, no matter what the result is.

items.q: Think of the highest goal you are currently pursuing in worldly life. In the light of these verses on liberation, does your aspiration move you towards freedom, or deeper into entanglement? Having understood this truth, how might your definition of 'success' or 'progress' evolve?
a: When I think about my goals, like doing well in my career, succeeding in an interview, and going deeper into my research and knowledge, I see that they are mostly focused on achievement and growth in the worldly sense. These goals are not wrong, but they can pull me into more attachment, pressure, and expectations, which means they can lead to deeper entanglement if I am not careful. Understanding these teachings, I realize that real progress is not just reaching these goals, but how I remain inside while pursuing them. My definition of success begins to change from just achieving results to staying calm, aware, and detached, while continuing my efforts without strong expectations.

parts.title: I. State whether you agree or disagree with each of the following statements, giving reasons for your answer (2 Marks Each)

items.q: It is not possible to attain liberation in the same birth by following the path of liberation mentioned in this pad. Shrimad Rajchandraji Himself says "janma tehna alp" - means few births, not no births
a: Disagree. The phrase janma tehna alp means few births, not that liberation cannot occur in the same birth. The Guru addresses the doubt of destroying infinite karmas in a short lifespan and provides a path to achieve it . Liberation depends on removing attachment, aversion, and ignorance, not on the number of births . If these causes are completely destroyed, liberation can be attained even in the present life.

items.q: Even though many souls have attained liberation through Bhaktimarg, insisting on it as the sole means of liberation is a cause of bondage.
a: Agree. While devotion (Bhaktimarg) can support spiritual progress and has helped many souls move toward liberation, insisting that it alone is the only path becomes a form of rigidity and wrong belief (mithyatva), which itself is a cause of bondage. The teachings clarify that liberation depends on destroying the true causes of bondage- attachment, aversion, and ignorance- not on adhering exclusively to any one external method or label. When one clings to a single path as superior and dismisses others, it reflects attachment and delusion, which bind further karmas instead of leading to freedom.

items.q: There is no rule that only those who follow the absolute path of liberation as explained by Shri Atmasiddhi Shastra can attain liberation.
a: Agree. Liberation is not limited to those who follow Shri Atmasiddhi Shastra specifically, because the path of liberation is universal in nature. The teachings emphasize inner transformation- removal of attachment, aversion, and ignorance-rather than adherence to a particular text, sect, or label. Different traditions may describe the same truth in different ways, but the underlying principles remain the same. Therefore, anyone who genuinely follows the true path by eliminating the causes of bondage and abiding in the Self can attain liberation, regardless of whether they formally follow this specific scripture.

items.q: It is not possible to end the cycle of transmigration by just ending the charitramohaniya karma, if darshanmohaniya karma is still present.
a: Agree. It is not possible to end the cycle of transmigration by eliminating only charitra-mohaniya (conduct-deluding karma) while darshan-mohaniya (faith-deluding karma) still remains. Darshan-mohaniya is the root cause that creates wrong belief and misunderstanding of reality. As long as this persists, true right faith (samyak darshan) does not arise, and without right faith, complete right conduct cannot be sustained. Even if outward conduct appears controlled, the inner delusion will continue to generate subtle attachment and aversion, leading to further bondage. Hence, both darshan-mohaniya and charitra-mohaniya must be destroyed to attain liberation.

items.q: Mokshbhaav means having the strong desire to attain the state of liberation.
a: Disagree. Mokshbhaav does not mean merely having a strong desire to attain liberation. It refers to the state of abiding in the pure Self (nijvas), free from identification with karmic impurities. Desire- even for liberation- is still a form of attachment and therefore part of bondage, not liberation. True mokshbhaav is the inner state where one is established in the Self, beyond attachment, aversion, and ignorance, which itself is the path to liberation.

parts.title: II. Answer in one Sentences (2 Marks Each)

items.q: Even though no karmic particle can stay attached to any soul forever, why has karmic bondage been continuing since time immemorial?
a: Karmic bondage has continued since time immemorial because, although old karmas get exhausted, new karmas keep getting bound due to persistent attachment, aversion, and ignorance.

items.q: Not just aversion (dwesh) but even attachment (raag) needs to be destroyed in order to attain liberation. Why?
a: Because both attachment (raag) and aversion (dwesh) are forms of passion that bind new karmas, so liberation is possible only when both are completely eliminated.

items.q: Mention any two qualities of the disciple seen through his usage of the word 'uday' twice (samju moksh upay toh, uday uday sadbhagya)
a: The use of “uday uday” reflects the disciple’s intense eagerness and enthusiastic faith (deep longing and optimism) to understand the path of liberation.

items.q: Why is the disciple sure in his heart that the Sadguru will be able to resolve his doubts regarding the sixth fundamental truth?
a: The disciple is sure because the Sadguru has already completely resolved his previous five doubts, giving him deep faith and confidence that the sixth will also be clarified.

items.q: Name any two of the five causes of bondage, and the corresponding virtues that destroy them.
a: Two causes of bondage are Mithyatva (wrong belief) and Kashay (passions); they are destroyed by Samyak Darshan (right faith) and Vitragta (dispassion) respectively.

items.q: What can 'bhagya' give, and what can 'sadbhagya' give?
a: Bhagya can give material comforts like wealth, health, and favorable situations, whereas Sadbhagya gives spiritual opportunities such as association with a Sadguru and the path to liberation.

items.q: Why are karmas of infinite types?
a: Karmas are of infinite types because the soul’s impure feelings (like attachment, aversion, and their countless variations) are infinite, and each such variation leads to different kinds of karmic bondage.

items.q: What are the two mistakes regarding our nature we have been making since time immemorial, due to which we are deluded regarding our true nature?
a: The two mistakes are identifying the Self with the non-self (body, mind, etc.) and considering the non-self as mine, which leads to delusion about our true nature.

items.q: Feelings of likes, dislikes arise within the soul. Yet, why are they called karmabhaav?
a: They are called karmabhaav because, although likes and dislikes arise within the soul, they are impure modifications caused by karmas and involve identification with them as I or mine, which is ignorance.

items.q: Explain the reason for the disciple's tinge of pessimism expressed in verse 95 (Tethi em janay chhe, maley na moksh upay ...).
a: The disciple feels pessimistic because, after seeing the vast accumulation of karmas and the presence of many conflicting paths and opinions, he is unable to identify an undisputed and reliable method of liberation, leading him to feel that the path may not be attainable.

parts.title: II. Answer in brief (3 Marks Each)

items.q: What does the word 'sahaj' in verse 97 (thashe moksh upayni, sahaj pratit e reet) mean? What virtues of the disciple are conveyed by the use of this word by the Sadguru? Explain the significance of the word ""thashe"" used by the Guru in this verse.
a: The word sahaj means natural, effortless, and with ease- indicating that the conviction of the path of liberation will arise without strain, just as the earlier five truths became clear. This reflects the disciple’s virtues of deep receptivity, faith, and inner readiness, due to which the understanding can arise smoothly. The word thashe (it will happen) signifies the Guru’s assurance and blessing, showing certainty that the disciple will definitely attain conviction about the path of liberation, thereby calming his doubts and strengthening his confidence.

items.q: Write the three main doubts of the disciple regarding the path of liberation.
a: The disciple has three main doubts regarding the path of liberation:
1. Karmas accumulated since infinite time are so vast that it seems impossible to destroy them within one short human lifespan.
2. There are numerous philosophies and paths claiming to be correct, making it difficult to decide which one is true.
3. There is confusion about eligibility- regarding caste, gender, and attire- leading to uncertainty about who can attain liberation and how.

items.q: Why is mohaniya karma called the king of karmas? Explain bodh and vitragta - the unfailing remedies to destroy the two types of mohaniya karma.
a: Mohaniya karma is called the king of karmas because it is the root cause of all bondage- it creates delusion, leading to wrong belief and wrong conduct, and thereby enables all other karmas to bind and operate. There are two types of mohaniya karma: darshan-mohaniya (deluding belief) and charitra-mohaniya (deluding conduct). Their unfailing remedies are: Bodh (true understanding) destroys darshan-mohaniya by giving right faith and correct perception of reality. Vitragta (dispassion) destroys charitra-mohaniya by removing attachment and aversion, leading to pure conduct.

items.q: Write any three of the five ways shown by Pujya Gurudevshri for developing forgiveness, overcoming anger.
a: Any three ways to develop forgiveness and overcome anger are:
1. Understanding (Bodh): Reflect that the other person is acting under their karmas and ignorance, just as we do, which reduces blame and anger.
2. Seeing one’s own faults: Instead of focusing on others’ mistakes, introspect and recognize one’s own weaknesses, which softens ego and anger.
3. Practicing equanimity (Samta): Maintain inner balance by not reacting immediately to situations, allowing anger to subside and forgiveness to arise naturally.

items.q: Explain the path of liberation using the methods of negative and positive assertion in verses 100 and 101 respectively.
a: The path of liberation is explained in two complementary ways: Negative assertion (Verse 100): Liberation is attained by withdrawing from the causes of bondage- attachment (raag), aversion (dwesh), and ignorance (ajnan). As these impurities are reduced and eliminated, one progresses on the path of liberation. Positive assertion (Verse 101): Liberation is attained by abiding in the pure nature of the Self, which is characterized by eternal existence, consciousness, and freedom from all illusion. Experiencing and remaining established in this true Self is the path of liberation.

parts.title: III. Self-Reflection and Inner Inquiry (3 marks each)

items.q: In moments of inner disturbance, how consistently are the four primary passions replaced by their corresponding pure virtues? Reflect on recent situations to see whether substitution actually occurred, or whether the passion merely changed its expression.
a: When I reflect on recent situations of inner disturbance, I notice that the four primary passions anger, pride, deceit and greed are not always consciously replaced by their corresponding virtues of forgiveness, humility, straightforwardness and contentment. At times I may suppress anger but it reappears as irritation or passive resistance or pride may shift into subtle comparison rather than true humility. This shows that the passion is not fully transformed but only changing form. Genuine progress requires mindful awareness in the moment and deliberate substitution with pure virtue rather than mere control or suppression.

items.q: How firmly are you convinced that factors such as caste, gender, social role, or external appearance have no bearing on liberation? Observe whether subtle pride, insecurity, or attachment still arises around these identities, and how you deal with it when it does.
a: When I reflect honestly, I am fairly convinced that caste, gender, social role, and external appearance have no real bearing on liberation, since liberation depends only on inner purity and the state of the soul. However, in day to day life, subtle pride, insecurity, or comparison can still arise around these identities, especially in social settings or when I feel judged or validated by others. Sometimes this shows up as a need for recognition or discomfort when these identities are challenged. In such moments, I try to pause, observe these reactions, and remind myself that they belong to the non self and are temporary modifications, not my true nature. By consciously correcting this identification and returning to a more neutral and aware state, I am gradually reducing attachment to these identities and strengthening my conviction in the true path.

items.q: Recall a recent disagreement in which you felt completely right and the other person entirely wrong. Can you examine whether this sense of absolute correctness was true clarity, or the quiet operation of delusion strengthening its own position?
a: When I reflect on a recent disagreement, I notice that my feeling of being completely right was not entirely true clarity but was influenced by subtle attachment and ego. At that moment, I was more focused on defending my viewpoint than understanding the other person’s perspective. This suggests that delusion was quietly strengthening its position by making my stance feel absolutely correct. With distance and reflection, I can see that my reaction was shaped by likes, dislikes, and identification, rather than pure understanding. This awareness helps me become more cautious in future situations, encouraging openness, humility, and a willingness to question my own certainty.

items.q: When your name, image, or behaviour is criticised, what exactly feels wounded within you? Using the crystal analogy, can you see that the soul only appears coloured due to karmic proximity, and that the perceived “hurt” does not belong to the soul itself?
a: When my name, image, or behaviour is criticised, what feels wounded is not the soul but the ego and the identity I have formed around how I want to be perceived. There is a strong sense of hurt because I unconsciously take that image to be me, so any criticism feels like a direct attack. On closer observation, this reaction is driven by attachment to reputation and a need for validation. Using the crystal analogy, I can understand that just as a crystal appears coloured due to nearby objects, the soul only appears affected because of karmic associations and identification with thoughts and emotions. The actual hurt belongs to the mind and personality, not to the pure Self. When I step back and observe this, I can see that the soul remains untouched, and the disturbance begins to weaken. This understanding helps me gradually reduce identification and respond with more awareness and steadiness.

items.q: When you experience anxiety, heaviness, or loss of inner balance, where does your effort naturally go first? Do you try to relieve the discomfort by increasing activity, prayer, or distraction—or do you attempt to trace the disturbance back to the specific attachment or expectation at its root?
a: When I experience anxiety, heaviness, or a loss of inner balance, my first tendency is often to move outward by engaging in activity, distraction, or even prayer to quickly ease the discomfort. While these can calm the surface level disturbance, I recognize that they do not always address the deeper cause. With greater awareness, I try to pause and look within to trace the disturbance back to a specific attachment, expectation, or desire that has been challenged. Often it is linked to wanting things to go a certain way, seeking validation, or resisting an outcome. By identifying this root, I can see how the imbalance was created and gradually loosen that attachment. This shift from external coping to internal inquiry helps me respond with more clarity and steadiness, leading to a more genuine and lasting sense of balance.

parts.title: I. Correct the understanding in the statements below (2 Marks Each)

items.q: Samyagdarshan brings along with it the annihilation of all deluding karmas simultaneously.
a: Samyagdarshan destroys faith-deluding karma, not all deluding karma at once. Conduct-deluding passions remain and are___________________________________________________________________________________________ gradually destroyed as right faith intensifies.

items.q: If delusion could dissolve instantly - like waking from a long dream, it would have already vanished by now.
a: Beginningless delusion can vanish instantly when true knowledge arises, but awakening requires the right causes, worthiness___________________________________________________________________________________________ and self-effort; its long past does not make awakening automatic.

items.q: When the false identification with the body ceases, all activities that were earlier instrumental in creating bondage stop.
a: False identification ceases, but bodily, mental and verbal activities may continue. The change is inward: the Enlightened One remains the knower-witness without doership or endurership.

items.q: The soul has infinite attributes, which cannot be expressed or experienced even in a million years.
a: The soul has infinite attributes and their glory cannot be exhausted by words, but they can be directly experienced; liberation fully manifests the soul's inherent qualities.

items.q: The definition of Omniscience (Kevaljnan) as "only constant knowledge only of one's own nature" contradicts the traditional, complete definition that the Omniscient One knows the entire universe (past, present, and future).
a: There is no contradiction. Traditionally, the Omniscient One knows all substances, places, times and modes. Shrimadji highlights the seeker's perspective: Kevaljnan is uninterrupted absorption in one's own true nature. Because knowledge is completely unobstructed, the entire universe is known naturally, without desire or outward effort.

parts.title: II. Answer in one Sentences (2 Marks Each)

items.q: What are the 2 meanings of 'antar daya'?
a: Antar daya means compassion for one's own soul suffering in transmigration, and inner compassion that naturally extends to___________________________________________________________________________________________ all living beings.

items.q: Why is the first phase of Samkit called Vyavahar Samkit?
a: It is called Vyavahar Samkit because right faith is still dependent on external support - the Sadguru, His words and teachings___________________________________________________________________________________________
rather than direct Self-experience.

items.q: Why is introspection necessary before contemplation?
a: Introspection first detects, negates and substitutes impure tendencies, cleansing the mind so contemplation can become___________________________________________________________________________________________ steady and fruitful.

items.q: Antarshodh unfolds in stages, beginning with introspection. What are the two subsequent stages?
Why are the Omniscient Ones called Liberated even though with the body (deh chhata nirvan)?
a: The Omniscient One is liberated while embodied because He is completely dispassionate and remains in uninterrupted Self-absorption, untouched by the body's association.

items.q: What is the difference in the experience of the soul of an Omniscient One (Kevaljnani) and the One who has attained the first phase of right belief (Vyavahar Samkiti)?
a: A Vyavahar Samkiti has faith in the Self based on the Sadguru's teachings but no direct Self-experience yet; a Kevaljnani has complete, uninterrupted experience and knowledge of the Self.

items.q: Why is Total Detachment (Vitragta) a precursor to Omniscience?
a: Total detachment is necessary because without attachment or aversion, nothing distracts or disturbs the soul, making uninterrupted Self-absorption and Omniscience possible.

items.q: Which action of the Guru towards the end of the dialogue show that He has no attachment for the disciple, and that His focus is only to get engrossed in the self?
a: After completing the disciple's guidance, the Guru stops speaking, assumes silence and effortlessly enters sahaj samadhi,___________________________________________________________________________________________ showing compassion without attachment and natural absorption in the Self.

items.q: How can we see the respect and reverence that Shrimad Rajchandraji has for the Enlightened Masters in the last verse of this section (verse 118)?
a: Shrimadji humbly says that the conclusions of all Enlightened Ones converge here, presenting the teaching not as His___________________________________________________________________________________________ personal doctrine but as their universal truth.

items.q: Name any four attributes of the soul shown by Shrimad Rajchandraji in these verses."
a: Any four: pure (shuddh), possessor of infinite knowledge (buddh), indivisible mass of consciousness (chaitanyaghan), self-luminous (swayamjyoti).

parts.title: II. Answer in brief (3 Marks Each)

items.q: How is nishchay samkit different from vyavahar samkit? Explain the phrase "jema bhed na paksh" used for nishchay samkit.
a: Vyavahar Samkit is right faith based on the Sadguru and His teachings; Nishchay/Shuddh Samkit arises from direct experience of the Self. 'Jema bhed na paksh' means that this pure Self-experience has no divisions based on religion, sect, caste, method___________________________________________________________________________________________ or external means - the experience of the true Self is the same.

items.q: Briefly explain the three attributes—anubhav, laksh, and pratit—that define the state of an Enlightened One as described in Verse 111 of the Atmasiddhi Shastra.
a: Anubhav is direct, thoughtless Self-experience when the Enlightened One is free from activities. Laksh is the constant inward awareness or inclination toward the Self while performing duties. Pratit is the firm conviction of the true Self that remains even___________________________________________________________________________________________ during sleep. Thus, in every state there is an unbroken connection with the Self through experience, awareness or conviction.

items.q: What is meant by the terms "flash" and "splash" in the context of Shuddh Samkit as described in Verse 110?
a: 'Flash' means the first direct glimpse of the pure Self may be brief or momentary. 'Splash' means that even this short experience leaves an unforgettable impression: it transforms the aspirant's vision and conviction permanently, even after the immediate experience subsides.

items.q: Based on Verse 116 of the Atmasiddhi Shastra, please explain the meanings of the statements "Ej dharmathi moksh chhe" and "Tu chho mokshswaroop". Why are these two statements considered reconcilable and not contradictory?
a: 'Ej dharmathi moksh chhe' means liberation is attained only through the dharma of ending false identification, retreating from impurity and abiding in the Self. 'Tu chho mokshswaroop' means the soul's eternal nature is already pure, free and of liberation-nature. They are reconcilable because liberation is eternally present as the soul's nature, while spiritual practice is required for that nature to become fully manifested as the liberated state.

items.q: What is the traditional concept of Kevaljnan (Omniscience)? How has Shrimadji defined Kevaljnan in these verses? Why are these two perspectives considered reconcilable rather than contradictory?
a: Traditionally, Kevaljnan means complete knowledge of all substances and all their modes across past, present and future. Shrimadji defines it spiritually as exclusive, uninterrupted knowledge and absorption in one's own true nature. These are not contradictory: the Omniscient One strives only for complete Self-absorption; when knowledge becomes totally unobstructed, the entire universe is illumined and known naturally, just as switching on a light reveals everything in a room.

parts.title: III. Self-Reflection and Inner Inquiry (3 marks each)

items.q: Reflect on the foundation of your spiritual journey. Just as a massive building like the Burj Khalifa requires an incredibly strong foundation to withstand storms, consider if you have cultivated the four essential virtues—pacified passions, exclusive desire for liberation, weariness of birth and rebirth, and inner compassion.
a: I can see that these four virtues are the real foundation and that I am still cultivating them. I need to reduce the intensity and duration of my passions, strengthen my desire for liberation, become genuinely weary of repeating the same inner cycles, and allow compassion to arise more naturally. My focus should be on making this foundation steady rather than rushing toward higher spiritual states.

items.q: Assess your inner receptivity during spiritual study. When you listen to the teachings of a Master, are you merely collecting words with your intellect, or are you absorbing them so deeply that they impregnate your soul with the potential for Self-realisation? Recall an incident when a spiritual truth truly clicked for you - did you manage to prolong that awareness, or did it quickly abort as you returned to worldly distractions?
a: At times I listen intellectually and feel inspired, but the awareness can fade when worldly activity resumes. I want to move from merely collecting teachings to absorbing and contemplating them deeply. When a truth clicks, I should revisit it, reflect on it and apply it so the inspiration matures into a lasting inner change instead of quickly disappearing.

items.q: Observe your state during moments of physical or emotional pain. Do you immediately become the "Bhokta" (endurer), feeling wounded and victimised by the situation? Can you recall a specific recent instance of discomfort and attempt to shift into the "jnatabhav" (knower-witness mode), recognising that while the body suffers, the soul remains an indifferent spectator like a shadow sweeping a courtyard without stirring the dust?
a: During pain or discomfort, my first reaction can still be to identify with it and become the bhokta. The practice is to notice that reaction and shift toward jnatabhav: the body or mind is experiencing the situation, while I try to remain the knower-witness. Even if I cannot remain there continuously, remembering this distinction can reduce reaction and attachment.

items.q: Recall an incident where you became deeply stressed or angry because of a professional or family obligation. In that moment, were you able to use the mantra "This is not my goal, it is only my role; I am a pure Soul"? How often do you allow your temporary roles to mask your true eternal nature like the millionaire who had mistakenly identified himself as a wretched rickshaw driver?
a: In stressful duties I can easily become absorbed in the role and temporarily forget the Self. The reminder, 'This is not my goal; this is only my role; I am a pure Soul,' helps separate responsibility from identification. I want to perform my roles sincerely while___________________________________________________________________________________________ remembering that they are temporary and are not my true identity.

items.q: Having been told that the conclusion of all Enlightened Masters converges in these teachings, are you dedicating yourself to the Guru's final instruction: deeply contemplate and realize the Self?
a: Yes. I want to treat 'Kar vichar to paam' as a practical instruction: not merely listening, but repeatedly contemplating the Guru's words and turning awareness inward toward the Self.

My effort should be to convert understanding into contemplation and contemplation into experience. The Guru has given the direction; now I must increase worthiness and purusharth, reduce false identification, practise the knower-witness mode and___________________________________________________________________________________________ sincerely seek abidance in the Self.

parts.title: I. Answer in one Sentence (2 Marks Each)

items.q: Why does the disciple refer to the Sadguru as Prabhu (God)?
a: After attaining Self-realisation, the disciple experiences the immeasurable grace of his Sadguru and develops such unwavering faith, love and reverence that he no longer sees Guru and God as separate; for him, his Sadguru Himself is Prabhu.

items.q: If activity is the soul's very nature, then why did the disciple say that there was no thought activity in the moments of his experience?
a: The soul never becomes inactive; in the nirvikalp state, thought activity ceases, but the soul remains active as the knower and enjoyer of its own pure modifications of consciousness.

items.q: How does the analogy of the sword and sheath (myan thaki tarvarvat) used by the disciple in this section reflect the devotion of the disciple for his Guru?
a: Just as a sword is distinct from its sheath, the disciple directly experiences himself as separate from the body and gratefully recognises that it was his Sadguru who gave him the spiritual vision to realise this distinction.

items.q: Write the verse or short meaning of the verse from the Sadguru's explanation of the third fundamental truth about the soul's doership that is reflected as the disciple's experience in verses 121 and 122?
a: When the soul is unaware of its true nature, it becomes the doer of karma; when it becomes aware of its true nature, it___________________________________________________________________________________________
becomes the doer of its own pure manifestations - exactly what the disciple now experiences in verses 121 and 122.

parts.title: II. Lets Dive deeper into the verse of this section (2 Marks Each)

items.q: Why does the disciple use the words "Charan kaney" instead of hastkamale (in Your Lotus hands) in verse 125? Shu Prabhu charan kaney dharu, atmathi sau heen; Te to prabhu e aapiyo, vartu charanadheen.
a: The disciple says 'Charan kaney' - at Your Lotus Feet - because his offering is not an ordinary exchange of gifts. Placing something at the Guru's Feet expresses complete humility, reverence and surrender. He does not seek recognition for what he offers; he simply wants to place everything at the Feet of his Prabhu.___________________________________________________________________________________________

items.q: Why does the disciple use the words "updeshthi" instead of "nimit thi" (instrumental cause) in verse 119? Sadguruna updesh thi, avyu apurva bhaan; Nijpada nijmahi lahyu, dur thayu ajnan.
a: From the path of knowledge, the Sadguru may technically be called the nimitta, since the disciple realised his own Self within himself. But bhakti does not say, 'You were merely an instrumental cause.' The disciple's heart feels, 'Gurudev, this happened because of You.' Therefore he says 'Sadguruna updeshthi,' giving the credit for his awakening to his Guru.

items.q: Why does the disciple use the words "nij shuddhata" instead of "Siddhashila par" (the physical place where the Siddhas reside) in verse 123? Moksh kahyo Siddhashila par, te paame te panth; Samjavyo sankshepma, sakal marg nirgranth.
a: Moksh is fundamentally a state, not a place. Simply being at Siddhashila does not define liberation; liberation means nij shuddhata - the completely pure and karmaless state of one's own soul. Therefore the disciple defines Moksh by the state___________________________________________________________________________________________ of the Self rather than by its physical location.

items.q: Why does the disciple use the word “das” three times in verse 126 - explain the two meanings of the words "das, das hu das chhu" explained by Pujya Gurudevshri. Aa dehadi aajthi, varto Prabhu adheen; Das, das hu das chhu, teh Prabhuno deen.
a: Gurudev explains the three 'das' in two ways. First, the disciple offers his mind, speech and body as servants of the Guru - he wants to think, speak and act according to His ajna. Second, it expresses increasing humility: 'I am the servant of the servant of Your servant.' Repeating 'das' shows how completely the disciple's ego has melted before his Guru.

parts.title: III. Answer in brief (3 Marks Each)

items.q: What is the meaning of the word "Aho!" that the disciple utters? For what did the disciple say the first pair of Aho! Aho!, and for what did he say the second pair of Aho! Aho!?
a: 'Aho!' is an exclamation of overwhelming wonder, reverence, love and gratitude - like saying 'Wow!' when an experience is greater than words. In 'Aho! Aho! Shri Sadguru,' the first pair arises in wonder at the greatness of his Sadguru, the boundless ocean of compassion. In 'Aho! Aho! Upkar,' the second pair arises in amazement at the immeasurable___________________________________________________________________________________________ benevolence the Guru has bestowed upon an unworthy disciple like him. Words fail him, so only 'Aho! Aho!' remains.

items.q: Explain the first line of verse 126 - Aa dehadi aajthi, varto Prabhu aadheen.
a: 'Aa dehadi' includes not only the physical body but also the mind, senses, intellect, speech, possessions and everything___________________________________________________________________________________________ the disciple considers 'mine.' 'Aajthi' means from this very moment - his surrender is immediate, not postponed. 'Varto Prabhu adheen' means that all of these should now operate according to his Prabhu's command. The same resources remain, but their direction and purpose change from 'for me' to 'for You.'

items.q: Explain: Nijpada nijmahi lahyu, door thayu ajnan.
a: 'Nijpada nijmahi lahyu' means the disciple realised his true Self within himself. The Guru did not create a new soul; the Self___________________________________________________________________________________________ had always existed within. Through the Sadguru's teachings, his vision changed and he directly experienced, 'I am the pure conscious Soul, not this body.' Thus 'door thayu ajnan' - his beginningless self-delusive ignorance and false identification of the Self with the non-Self were destroyed.

items.q: Narrate the disciple's journey of deciding what he should offer at his Sadguru's Lotus feet, through the words: “Atmathi sau heen”, “Te toh Prabhue aapiyo”, “Vartu charanadheen”.
a: Overwhelmed by his Guru's immeasurable benevolence, the disciple wonders what he could possibly offer in return. First he considers worldly objects, but realises 'Atmathi sau heen' - everything is inferior to the Soul, so no material gift is worthy enough. He then thinks of offering the most precious thing, his Self-realisation, but realises 'Te toh Prabhue aapiyo' -___________________________________________________________________________________________ awareness of that very Self was bestowed upon him through his Prabhu. How could he repay the Guru by giving His own gift back to Him? With no object worthy enough to offer, he finally offers himself: 'Vartu charanadheen.' He resolves that his entire life will now be lived under the Guru's command. Thus gratitude develops into surrender, and surrender into a life of ajna and seva.

parts.title: IV. Self-Reflection and Inner Inquiry (3 marks each)

items.q: Evaluate your current spiritual efforts - are you focusing on informational knowledge or experiential conviction?
a: I feel that much of my spiritual effort is still at the level of informational and intellectual knowledge. Through satsang and studying Atmasiddhi, I may understand concepts such as dehadhyas, the Six Fundamental Truths and the distinction between the body and Soul, but understanding them is not the same as experiencing them. This section reminds me that___________________________________________________________________________________________ the disciple did not stop at understanding Gurudev's words; he contemplated them until they became his own experience. I want to move from simply asking, 'What did I learn?' toward asking, 'What did I actually take within and apply?' My aspiration is for Gurudev's teachings to gradually move from information to conviction and eventually toward experience.

items.q: Think of a time you were asked to adjust to someone else's expectations or instructions. Did your ego react with tantrums, or were you able to embody the modesty depicted in these verses?
a: There have definitely been situations, especially while working with others, where an instruction did not match how I wanted something to be done. My first internal reaction can sometimes be to defend my own idea, question why I should change, or feel that my way makes more sense. That shows me how quickly the 'I' can come forward. Verse 126 gives me___________________________________________________________________________________________ a different standard: 'Prabhu adheen.' True surrender cannot exist only when the instruction already agrees with me. I want to become more aware of that first ego reaction, reduce my insistence, and learn to respond with greater humility, flexibility and willingness to serve.

items.q: Examine your valuation of worldly pleasures compared to the refuge of an Enlightened Master. If you were offered the entire universe or even the joys of heaven in exchange for it, would you find them to be petty or like dirt? Do you acknowledge that Self-realization is the only wish-fulfilling tree that can truly rejuvenate you and annihilate all present and future suffering?
a: Intellectually, I understand that no worldly possession or pleasure can compare with the refuge of an Enlightened Master, but I cannot claim that my choices always reflect that understanding. The world can still feel extremely valuable when I am caught in it. These verses remind me that even the entire universe or the pleasures of heaven are temporary, while the Sadguru reveals the Self and shows the path that can permanently end suffering. Self-realisation is therefore the true___________________________________________________________________________________________ wish-fulfilling tree because it does not merely satisfy another temporary desire; it reveals the source of bliss within and leads toward freedom from all bondage. I want my valuation to gradually shift so that Guru's refuge and inner transformation become more precious to me than temporary worldly pleasures.

items.q: Look at your prayers and devotional practices. Are they mechanical recitations in the third person, or are they personalised commitments made to a Lord who is present in your heart? Do you recognize that the most important ingredient of your prayer is faith?
a: At times my prayers can become mechanical, where I recite the words correctly without fully connecting my heart to their meaning. This section teaches me to make prayer personal - to move from 'that Guru' to 'my Gurudev,' and from 'that Lord' to 'You.' When I say that I surrender or that I am Your servant, I want it to become more than something I recite; I want it to___________________________________________________________________________________________ influence how I think, speak and act afterward. The most important ingredient is faith, because without genuine faith the words remain only words. My aspiration is to pray with the awareness that Gurudev is present in my heart and to let every prayer become a sincere commitment to live more according to His ajna.

bonus.title: Connect the Verses
bonus.intro: Each question has two distinct hints originating from two separate verses of the Upsamhar (Conclusion) section. Both hints point to the same core Gujarati word from the original verses.

example.h1: The viewpoint which is kept in perfect harmony with the absolute viewpoint, rather than being stated one-sidedly in Shri Atmasiddhi Shastra.
example.h2: The sad………… which is entirely absent in those who harbor imagined, sectarian distinctions of creed.

items.h1: Those who have been in the past, are in the present, and will be in the future, treading the exact same path of liberation.
items.h2: The One Who is beyond the body despite being in an embodied condition, and at Whose lotus feet innumerable salutations are offered.

items.h1: The specific type of "effort" you are instructed to make if you truly desire the supreme truth without making excuses.
items.h2: One of the seven cardinal virtues that is constantly awake in the heart of a true seeker, listed alongside compassion, peace, and equanimity.

items.h1: The expert physician Who is uniquely capable of curing the deadly disease of self-delusion.
items.h2: The one whose commands serve as a powerful instrumental cause for our liberation.

items.h1: That viewpoint which you must keep in focus without giving up your spiritual means.
items.h2: That viewpoint which is considered entirely futile or unbeneficial if you lack the true awareness of the Self.

items.h1: That which remains perfectly intact deep inside a hypocrite, even while he verbally preaches lofty spiritual knowledge.
items.h2: That which must be either totally destroyed or highly subsided to truly verify the enlightened state.
